school-c9-social-a.title: Class 9 Social Science · History (India and the Contemporary World – I)
school-c9-social-a.description: Chapter-by-chapter Class 9 History: the French Revolution, socialism and the Russian Revolution, Nazism, forest societies and pastoralists — explained fully with solved answers, common mistakes and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · The French Revolution
courses.summary: Why France exploded in 1789, how the monarchy fell, what the Jacobins and the Terror were, and the ideas of liberty and equality the Revolution left to the world.
outcomes: Learners can describe French society under the Old Regime and its three estates
Learners can sequence the main events of 1789–1815
Learners can explain the role of philosophers and the middle class
Learners can evaluate what the Revolution changed for women, slaves and everyday life

lessons.title: French society in the late 18th century

scenes.text: In 1788 Jacques, a peasant near Paris, pays rent to the lord, a tenth of his grain to the Church, and the taille to the state.
Bread prices jump after a bad harvest. His wages have not risen. He wonders why the rich priests and nobles pay almost nothing.

steps.title: The Old Regime
steps.body:
In 1774 **Louis XVI** of the Bourbon family became king of France. He inherited an **empty treasury**: long wars and help to the thirteen American colonies in their war against Britain had doubled France's debt to more than 2 billion livres.

French society before 1789 is called the **Old Regime (ancien régime)**. It was divided into three **estates**:
- **First Estate** – clergy (Church)
- **Second Estate** – nobility
- **Third Estate** – everyone else: big businessmen, merchants, lawyers, court officials, peasants, artisans, landless labourers and servants

The first two estates were born into **privileges**, the most important being **exemption from taxes** paid to the state.

steps.title: Who paid what
steps.body:
- **Tithes**: a tax the Church collected from peasants — one-tenth of agricultural produce.
- **Taille**: a direct tax paid to the state, only by the Third Estate.
- **Indirect taxes** on everyday goods like salt and tobacco.
- Feudal dues to nobles, and unpaid labour (in the lord's house, fields, army or road building).

The peasants made up about 90% of the population, yet only a small number owned the land they cultivated; about 60% of land was owned by nobles, the Church and richer Third Estate members.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What was a 'subsistence crisis'? Why did it happen in France? (3 marks)**
- Step 1 – Define: a situation where the basic means of livelihood are endangered.
- Step 2 – Cause: population rose from about 23 million in 1715 to 28 million in 1789, so demand for grain rose faster than production.
- Step 3 – Effect: bread prices rose quickly, wages did not keep pace, and drought or hail made things worse. The gap between rich and poor widened.

**Q2. Why was the Third Estate angry? (3 marks)**
- It alone paid taxes to the state (taille) and tithes to the Church.
- It had no privileges, though it did most of the work.
- Its richer members (the new middle class) were educated and wanted position by merit, not birth.

steps.title: A growing middle class and new ideas
steps.body:
Merchants, manufacturers, lawyers and administrators grew rich through trade and expanding industries (like woollen and silk textiles). They believed no group should be privileged by birth.

Philosophers shaped their thinking:
- **John Locke** (*Two Treatises of Government*) rejected the **divine and absolute right** of the monarch.
- **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** (*The Social Contract*) proposed government based on a contract between people and their representatives.
- **Montesquieu** (*The Spirit of the Laws*) proposed dividing power among the **legislature, executive and judiciary**.

These ideas spread in salons, coffee-houses, books and newspapers, often read aloud to people who could not read.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the First Estate was the nobility — it was the **clergy**. Nobility = Second Estate.
- Writing that the Third Estate was only peasants — it also included rich merchants and lawyers.
- Mixing up the books: *Social Contract* = Rousseau; *Spirit of the Laws* = Montesquieu; *Two Treatises* = Locke.
- Forgetting that tithes went to the **Church**, taille to the **state**.

activity.prompt: Match each thinker with the idea or book
pairs: Division of power into three organs

quiz.q: Who belonged to the First Estate?
quiz.why: In the old French society the clergy formed the First Estate, nobles the Second, and the rest (peasants, merchants, workers) the Third. So the Church people were the First Estate.

quiz.q: Which tax was paid directly to the state by the Third Estate?
quiz.why: The taille was a direct tax paid to the state, and it fell on the Third Estate. The tithe went to the Church, and corvée was forced labour; the livre was a currency.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'The Spirit of the Laws'?
quiz.why: Montesquieu wrote 'The Spirit of the Laws' and proposed dividing power among the legislature, executive and judiciary. Rousseau wrote 'The Social Contract' and Locke 'Two Treatises of Government'.

quiz.q: A main reason for France's empty treasury under Louis XVI was:
options: Long wars including aid to American colonies
quiz.why: War expenses, including helping the American colonies, pushed debt above 2 billion livres.

quiz.q: A subsistence crisis means:
options: The basic means of livelihood are endangered
quiz.why: A subsistence crisis means ordinary people's basic means of survival, such as food, are in danger. In France, a rising population, poor harvests and costly bread caused this.

lessons.title: 1789: the outbreak of the Revolution

story.title: A locked hall, a tennis court

scenes.text: 20 June 1789. Delegates of the Third Estate find their meeting hall at Versailles locked.
They gather in an indoor tennis court and swear not to separate until France has a constitution.

steps.title: The Estates General
steps.body:
To raise new taxes, Louis XVI called the **Estates General** — a political body of the three estates — on **5 May 1789**. It had last met in **1614**.

Each estate traditionally had **one vote**. The Third Estate (about 600 members) demanded voting **by each member**, so each member would have one vote. When the king refused, its members walked out.

On **20 June 1789** they assembled in an indoor tennis court at Versailles, declared themselves the **National Assembly**, and took the **Tennis Court Oath**. Leaders: **Mirabeau** (a noble) and **Abbé Sieyès** (a priest, who wrote the pamphlet *What is the Third Estate?*).

steps.title: 14 July 1789 and the Great Fear
steps.body:
Rumours spread that the king would order troops to fire on citizens. On **14 July 1789** an agitated crowd stormed and destroyed the **Bastille**, a fortress-prison hated as a symbol of the king's despotic power.

In the countryside, rumours that lords' bands were coming to destroy crops led to the **Great Fear**: peasants attacked chateaux, looted grain and burnt records of manorial dues. Many nobles fled.

On **4 August 1789** the Assembly abolished the feudal system of obligations and taxes, abolished tithes and confiscated Church lands.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why was the Bastille stormed? (2 marks)**
It stood for the king's despotic power; people feared troops would be ordered to fire on them, so they attacked it on 14 July 1789.

**Q2. Describe the Tennis Court Oath. (3 marks)**
- Step 1 – Background: the king refused vote-per-member at the Estates General.
- Step 2 – Event: on 20 June 1789 Third Estate representatives met in an indoor tennis court at Versailles.
- Step 3 – Significance: they declared themselves the National Assembly and swore not to disperse till they drafted a constitution limiting the monarch's powers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Estates General was **not** an elected parliament with law-making power; it only met when the king called it.
- The Bastille was stormed on **14 July** (French National Day), not 4 August.
- Sieyès wrote *What is the Third Estate?* — not *The Social Contract*.

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: **5 May → 20 June → 14 July → 4 August** (1789): meet, swear, storm, abolish.

activity.prompt: Put the events of 1789 in order

events.text: Tennis Court Oath; National Assembly declared

quiz.q: When had the Estates General last met before 1789?
quiz.why: The Estates General had not met since 1614, so it was a rarely used body. Louis XVI called it in 1789 to approve new taxes.

quiz.q: What did the Third Estate demand at the Estates General?
quiz.why: The Third Estate wanted each member to have one vote, since it had far more members than the other two estates combined. The old system gave one vote per estate, which let the two privileged estates win.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'What is the Third Estate?'
quiz.why: Abbé Sieyès, a priest, wrote the pamphlet 'What is the Third Estate?', which argued that the common people were the real nation. Rousseau, Voltaire and Montesquieu wrote other works.

quiz.q: The Great Fear refers to:
options: Peasant panic and attacks on chateaux in 1789
quiz.why: The Great Fear was the rural panic of 1789, when rumours of brigands made peasants attack chateaux, loot grain and burn documents recording feudal dues. It was not the Terror, which came later.

quiz.q: On 4 August 1789 the Assembly:
quiz.why: On the night of 4 August 1789, the National Assembly abolished feudal obligations and tithes, and Church land was later taken over. Executing the king and crowning Napoleon happened later.

lessons.title: From constitutional monarchy to republic and Terror

scenes.text: Pierre, a 30-year-old shopkeeper who pays taxes, is told he is an 'active citizen' and may vote in 1791.
His wife Marie, who also works in the shop, is told she is a 'passive citizen'. She joins a women's club to protest.

steps.title: The Constitution of 1791
steps.body:
The National Assembly completed a constitution in **1791**. It made France a **constitutional monarchy**: the king's powers were divided among the legislature, executive and judiciary.
- Laws were made by the **National Assembly**, which was **indirectly elected**.
- Only **active citizens** could vote: men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least 3 days of a labourer's wage. The rest — men without such property, and all women — were **passive citizens**.
- It began with the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen** (1789): life, freedom of speech and opinion, equality before law as natural and inalienable rights.

steps.title: War, Jacobins and the Republic
steps.body:
- **April 1792**: the Assembly declared war against **Prussia and Austria**. Volunteers marched singing the *Marseillaise*, composed by Roget de L'Isle.
- The **Jacobin club** (led by **Maximilian Robespierre**) drew in small shopkeepers, artisans and workers. Many wore long striped trousers and were called **sans-culottes** ('without knee breeches').
- **August 1792**: Jacobins stormed the Tuileries palace and held the king hostage.
- Elections were then held in which **all men over 21**, regardless of wealth, could vote. The new assembly, the **Convention**, abolished the monarchy on **21 September 1792** and declared France a **republic**.
- Louis XVI was executed for treason in **January 1793**; Queen Marie Antoinette shortly after.

steps.title: The Reign of Terror and the Directory
steps.body:
**1793–1794** is called the **Reign of Terror**. Robespierre followed a policy of severe control: people he saw as enemies of the republic were arrested and tried by a revolutionary tribunal; many were executed by guillotine. He set price ceilings on wages and prices, rationed meat and bread, forced peasants to sell grain at fixed prices, banned expensive white flour (everyone ate the 'equality bread'), and replaced Monsieur/Madame with **Citoyen/Citoyenne**.

Robespierre was convicted and executed in **July 1794**. A new constitution then created two elected councils which appointed a five-member executive called the **Directory**. Political instability under the Directory paved the way for the rise of **Napoleon Bonaparte**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Distinguish active and passive citizens. (2 marks)**
Active citizens: men above 25 paying taxes equal to at least 3 days' wages — they could vote. Passive citizens: all others including all women — no vote.

**Q2. Why is 1793–94 called the Reign of Terror? (3 marks)**
- Robespierre's government used severe control and punishment.
- Nobles, clergy, members of other parties and even his own party who disagreed were arrested and many guillotined.
- Laws on prices, rations and dress were enforced strictly; the period ended with his own execution in July 1794.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The 1791 Constitution did **not** abolish monarchy — the Convention did, in September 1792.
- 'Sans-culottes' means *without knee breeches* (the fashion of nobles), not 'without clothes'.
- Universal adult *male* suffrage came in 1792 elections — women still could not vote.

activity.prompt: Under the 1791 Constitution, sort these people

items.text: A landless servant aged 50 who paid no taxes

quiz.q: The 1791 Constitution made France a:
quiz.why: The 1791 Constitution kept the king but limited his powers by dividing them among the legislature, executive and judiciary. A king with limited power under a constitution is a constitutional monarchy.

quiz.q: Who led the Jacobin club?
quiz.why: Maximilian Robespierre led the Jacobin club, the most famous political club of the Revolution. Mirabeau was a moderate leader, and Louis XVI was the king.

quiz.q: France was declared a republic on:
quiz.why: The Convention abolished the monarchy and declared France a republic on 21 September 1792. The king was executed in January 1793, and the Bastille fell on 14 July 1789.

quiz.q: The Directory was:
quiz.why: After Robespierre's fall, two councils appointed a five-member executive called the Directory.

quiz.q: The patriotic song 'Marseillaise' was composed by:
quiz.why: Roget de L'Isle composed the song in 1792. Volunteers from Marseilles sang it as they marched to Paris, so it became known as the Marseillaise and later France's national anthem.

lessons.title: Women, slavery, everyday life and the legacy

scenes.text: Olympe de Gouges reads the Declaration of the Rights of Man and notices it says nothing about women.
She writes her own Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen and sends it to the queen and the Assembly.

steps.title: Did women gain?
steps.body:
Most Third Estate women worked as seamstresses, laundresses, sellers or domestic servants, with little education. They formed political clubs; about 60 women's clubs came up in French cities, the best known being the **Society of Revolutionary and Republican Women**.

Gains: state schools and compulsory schooling for all girls, no forced marriage, marriage as a contract, **divorce made legal**, and women could train for jobs and run small businesses.

Under the Terror women's clubs were closed and many prominent women, including **Olympe de Gouges**, were executed. French women finally won the **right to vote in 1946**.

steps.title: Abolition of slavery
steps.body:
French colonies in the Caribbean (Martinique, Guadeloupe, San Domingo) depended on enslaved Africans for tobacco, indigo, sugar and coffee. Port cities like Bordeaux and Nantes grew rich on the slave trade.
- **1794**: the Convention freed all slaves in French overseas possessions.
- About ten years later **Napoleon reintroduced slavery**.
- Slavery was **finally abolished in French colonies in 1848**.

steps.title: Everyday life and the legacy
steps.body:
After 1789, **censorship was abolished**; newspapers, pamphlets, books and printed pictures flooded towns; plays, songs and festive processions spread ideas of liberty and justice.

**Napoleon** crowned himself Emperor in **1804** and conquered much of Europe, introducing laws such as protection of private property and a uniform system of weights and measures (the decimal system). He was finally defeated at **Waterloo in 1815**.

**Legacy**: liberty and democratic rights spread across Europe in the 19th century; feudal systems were abolished; colonised peoples (for example **Tipu Sultan** and **Rammohan Roy** in India) drew on these ideas.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Which laws improved women's lives after the Revolution? (3 marks)**
Compulsory schooling for girls; marriage as a free contract and no forced marriage; legal divorce; right to train for jobs and run small businesses.

**Q2. Trace the history of slavery in French colonies. (3 marks)**
1794 – abolished by the Convention → about 10 years later reintroduced by Napoleon → 1848 – finally abolished.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Women did **not** get the vote in the Revolution — only in **1946**.
- Slavery was not abolished once and for all in 1794; remember the 1848 date.
- Napoleon was a product of the Revolution's instability but was **not** a Jacobin leader of the Terror.

statements.s: French women won the right to vote in 1946.
statements.why: This was a long struggle that continued after the Revolution.

statements.s: Napoleon permanently ended slavery.
statements.why: He reintroduced it; final abolition came in 1848.

statements.s: Censorship was abolished after 1789.
statements.why: The Declaration made freedom of speech a natural right.

statements.s: Divorce was made legal for French women during the Revolution.
statements.why: It was one of the laws that improved women's lives.

quiz.q: Who wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen?
quiz.why: Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen because the 1789 Declaration of Rights of Man left women out. She demanded equal rights for women.

quiz.q: When was slavery finally abolished in French colonies?
quiz.why: Slavery was abolished in 1794 by the Convention, but Napoleon brought it back. It was finally abolished in French colonies in 1848.

quiz.q: Napoleon was finally defeated at:
quiz.why: Napoleon was finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. The Bastille and Versailles are not battles he lost, and Austerlitz was one of his victories.

quiz.q: Which Indian figure was influenced by revolutionary ideas from France?
quiz.why: Tipu Sultan was inspired by revolutionary France: he planted a tree of liberty and became a member of a Jacobin club. Akbar, Ashoka and Shivaji lived long before this.

quiz.q: Port towns that grew rich on the slave trade were:
quiz.why: Bordeaux and Nantes were French ports whose merchants grew rich on the slave trade, as ships carried enslaved Africans to the Caribbean colonies. Paris and Lyon are not port towns.

questions.q: The Second Estate consisted of:
questions.why: The nobility formed the Second Estate in France's old society. The clergy were the First Estate, while peasants and merchants belonged to the Third Estate.

questions.q: The Bastille was stormed on:
questions.why: The Bastille, a prison fortress seen as a symbol of royal despotism, was stormed by the Parisian crowd on 14 July 1789. This date is now France's national day.

questions.q: Louis XVI became king in:
questions.why: Louis XVI became king in 1774 at the age of 20. The Revolution broke out in 1789, and he was executed in 1793, so those years are not the start of his rule.

questions.q: Which book argued for dividing power among legislature, executive and judiciary?
questions.why: Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of the Laws' argued that power should be divided among the legislature, executive and judiciary. 'The Social Contract' is Rousseau's work on popular sovereignty.

questions.q: Who could vote under the 1791 Constitution?
options: Men over 25 paying taxes worth at least 3 days' wages
questions.why: Under the 1791 Constitution only 'active citizens', men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least 3 days of a labourer's wages, could vote. Women and poorer men were 'passive citizens'.

questions.q: Sans-culottes were:
options: Jacobin supporters, often poorer, who wore long striped trousers
questions.why: Sans-culottes, meaning 'without knee breeches', were poorer people who wore long striped trousers, unlike nobles who wore knee breeches. They supported the Jacobins.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Third Estate walked out of the Estates General. Reason (R): The king rejected voting by each member.
options: Both A and R true; R explains A
Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true. The Third Estate walked out because the king refused its demand for one vote per member, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which happened FIRST?
options: War declared on Prussia and Austria
questions.why: April 1792 war → Sept 1792 republic → Jan 1793 execution → July 1794 Robespierre.

questions.q: Case: In 1793 a baker is forced to bake only one kind of bread from mixed grain and to sell at a fixed price. This reflects:
questions.why: Forcing bakers to bake one 'equality bread' and fixing prices was part of Robespierre's Terror-era controls. The Old Regime and the Directory did not do this, and Napoleon's Code dealt with civil law.

questions.q: Which right was NOT included in the Declaration of the Rights of Man as a natural right?
questions.why: The Declaration of the Rights of Man guaranteed rights such as life, speech and equality before law, but women were not given the vote. That is why Olympe de Gouges protested.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Revolution gave women equal political rights. Reason (R): Women's clubs were closed during the Terror.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Women did not get equal political rights (vote only in 1946); clubs were indeed closed.

questions.q: If France's population rose from 23 million to 28 million between 1715 and 1789, the percentage increase is about:
questions.why: Increase = 28 − 23 = 5 million. Percentage = 5 ÷ 23 × 100 ≈ 21.7%, about 22%. Always divide by the original value (23), not the new one.

questions.q: Why did the middle class lead the Revolution rather than the peasants alone?
options: They were educated, wealthy and believed position should depend on merit
questions.why: The middle class was educated and wealthy, and believed that position should depend on merit, not birth. This made them the leaders and thinkers of the Third Estate, though they were not the majority.

questions.q: Case: A ruler crowns himself emperor, conquers neighbours, introduces uniform weights and measures and protects private property, but reintroduces slavery. Who and when?
questions.why: Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804, conquered neighbouring lands, brought uniform weights, measures and the Civil Code protecting property, and reintroduced slavery. Louis XVI and Robespierre did not do these things.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why the Directory fell?
options: Political instability let a military dictator, Napoleon, rise
questions.why: The Directory was weak and unstable, with conflicts among its members and the people. This let the military leader Napoleon take power in 1799. It did not free slaves or abolish the monarchy.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Socialism in Europe and the Russian Revolution
courses.summary: Liberals, radicals and conservatives; the rise of socialism; and how Russia moved from the Tsar to the Bolsheviks, collectivisation and a global impact.
outcomes: Learners can compare liberal, radical and conservative ideas
Learners can explain socialist ideas of Owen, Blanc and Marx
Learners can sequence the 1905, February 1917 and October 1917 events
Learners can evaluate Stalin's collectivisation and the Revolution's global influence

lessons.title: Liberals, radicals, conservatives and the rise of socialism

story.title: Three friends argue in a café

scenes.text: Paris, 1830s. Henri, a liberal, wants a parliament but only property owners voting.
Lucie, a radical, says every adult, women too, must vote. Old Gaston, a conservative, says change must be slow and respect tradition.

steps.title: Three political trends
steps.body:
After the French Revolution, Europeans debated how society should change.
- **Liberals**: wanted religious tolerance, an elected parliamentary government and an independent judiciary; opposed the uncontrolled power of rulers. But they were **not democrats**: they wanted only men of property to vote and did not want women to vote.
- **Radicals**: wanted government based on the majority of a country's population; supported women's suffrage; opposed privileges of great landowners and factory owners, though not private property itself.
- **Conservatives**: opposed radicals and liberals; after the Revolution they accepted some change, but wanted the past respected and change to be slow.

steps.title: Industrial society and social change
steps.body: Industrialisation brought men, women and children into factories with long working hours and poor wages; unemployment was common. Liberals and radicals, often property owners themselves, believed in individual effort and merit. Some nationalists, like **Giuseppe Mazzini** in Italy, conspired with radicals to create nation-states.

steps.title: Socialism
steps.body:
**Socialists** were against private property, which they saw as the root of social ills: owners cared only for profit, not for the workers who made it.
- **Robert Owen** (English manufacturer) tried to build a cooperative community called **New Harmony** in Indiana, USA.
- **Louis Blanc** (France) wanted the government to encourage cooperatives and replace capitalist enterprises.
- **Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** argued that industrial society was capitalist; workers had to overthrow capitalism and build a **communist society** where all property was socially controlled.

Socialists formed the **Second International**. Workers in England and Germany formed associations for better conditions; the **Labour Party** in Britain and the **Socialist Party** in France were formed by 1905.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why were liberals not 'democrats'? (2 marks)**
They supported an elected parliament but believed only men of property should vote, and opposed universal adult franchise including votes for women.

**Q2. How did Marx's view differ from Owen's? (3 marks)**
- Owen: build voluntary cooperative communities (New Harmony).
- Marx: capitalism exploits workers; workers must overthrow it to create a communist society with property under social control.
- So Owen sought reform by example; Marx sought a revolutionary transformation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking radicals opposed **all** private property — they only opposed concentration of property in a few hands.
- Calling liberals supporters of universal adult franchise — they were not.
- Placing New Harmony in Britain — it was in **Indiana, USA**.

activity.prompt: Which group held this view?

items.text: Only men of property should vote
Women should have the right to vote
Change should be slow and respect the past
Private property is the root of social ills
Religious tolerance and an independent judiciary

quiz.q: Who set up the cooperative community 'New Harmony'?
quiz.why: Robert Owen, a British industrialist, set up the cooperative community 'New Harmony' in Indiana, USA. Louis Blanc and Marx are linked with other socialist ideas.

quiz.q: Which group supported women's suffrage?
quiz.why: Radicals wanted a nation where government was based on the majority and supported votes for women. Liberals and conservatives were not in favour of this in the same way.

quiz.q: Marx believed workers must overthrow:
quiz.why: Marx held that capitalism exploited workers, so they must overthrow it and build a communist society. He did not want to overthrow socialism, which was his aim.

quiz.q: Louis Blanc wanted:
quiz.why: Louis Blanc wanted the government to promote cooperatives and replace capitalist enterprises with collective ones run by those who worked in them.

quiz.q: The Labour Party was formed in:
quiz.why: The Labour Party was formed in Britain, in the early 1900s (by 1905), by trade unionists and socialists to fight for workers' rights. Germany had its own Social Democratic Party.

lessons.title: Russia under the Tsar and the 1905 Revolution

scenes.text: January 1905. Workers led by Father Gapon march peacefully to the Winter Palace with a petition.
Police and Cossacks attack the procession; over 100 workers are killed. Strikes spread across Russia.

steps.title: The Russian Empire in 1914
steps.body:
In 1914 **Tsar Nicholas II** ruled Russia and its empire, including present-day Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, parts of Poland, Ukraine and Belarus, reaching the Pacific, and Central Asian states, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan. The majority religion was **Russian Orthodox Christianity**.

**About 85%** of Russians earned their living from agriculture. Peasants cultivated for the market and for their needs; they had no respect for nobility and pooled land in a **commune (mir)** that divided it periodically. Industry was found in pockets (St Petersburg and Moscow); workers were divided by skill but united in strikes.

steps.title: Socialism in Russia
steps.body: All political parties were illegal before 1914. Socialists founded the **Russian Social Democratic Workers' Party in 1898**. It split into the **Bolsheviks**, led by **Vladimir Lenin** (a disciplined party of revolutionaries), and the **Mensheviks** (an open party, like Germany's). The **Socialist Revolutionary Party (1900)** worked for peasants' rights and wanted nobles' land transferred to peasants.

steps.title: 1905 and the Duma
steps.body:
In 1904 prices of essential goods rose quickly and real wages fell. When four members of the Assembly of Russian Workers were dismissed at the Putilov Iron Works, a strike followed.

On **Bloody Sunday** (January 1905) a procession led by **Father Gapon** reached the Winter Palace; police attacked, killing over 100 and wounding about 300. Strikes, university closures and demands for a constituent assembly followed — the **1905 Revolution**.

The Tsar allowed an elected consultative parliament, the **Duma**, but dismissed the first one within 75 days and the second within three months, then packed the third with conservatives.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why is the 1905 event called Bloody Sunday? (2 marks)**
A peaceful workers' procession to the Winter Palace was attacked by police on a Sunday; over 100 were killed and about 300 wounded.

**Q2. Compare Bolsheviks and Mensheviks. (3 marks)**
- Bolsheviks (Lenin): a disciplined, small party of revolutionaries; believed a parliament was not possible under the Tsar.
- Mensheviks: an open party like in Germany, willing to work within a parliamentary system.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The 1905 Revolution did **not** overthrow the Tsar — that happened in February 1917.
- The Duma was a consultative parliament the Tsar repeatedly dismissed; it did not hold real power.
- Lenin led the **Bolsheviks**, not the Mensheviks.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning

quiz.q: About what share of Russians depended on agriculture in 1914?
quiz.why: In 1914 about 85% of Russians earned a living from agriculture, a much higher share than in Germany or France. Russia was still a mostly farming country.

quiz.q: The Russian Social Democratic Workers' Party was founded in:
quiz.why: The Russian Social Democratic Workers' Party was founded in 1898 by socialists who followed Marx's ideas. 1905 and 1917 were years of revolution.

quiz.q: Who led the procession on Bloody Sunday?
quiz.why: Father Gapon led the workers' procession to the Winter Palace in 1905, which was attacked by the Tsar's troops. The event was called Bloody Sunday.

quiz.q: After 1905 the Tsar allowed:
quiz.why: After the 1905 revolution the Tsar allowed an elected consultative Duma, but kept dismissing it. He did not grant a republic or universal suffrage.

quiz.q: The majority religion of Russia was:
quiz.why: Most Russians followed Russian Orthodox Christianity, the faith of the Tsar's Church. Catholicism, Islam and Judaism were followed by minorities.

lessons.title: War and the revolutions of 1917

scenes.text: Winter 1917. In Petrograd women stand in long bread queues in the freezing cold.
On 23 February, International Women's Day, women lead factory strikes. Within days soldiers join them and the Tsar abdicates.

steps.title: The First World War and Russia
steps.body:
In 1914 war broke out between the Central Powers (Germany, Austria, Turkey) and the Allies (France, Britain, Russia). The war became unpopular; the Tsar refused to consult the main parties in the Duma. St Petersburg was renamed **Petrograd** (anti-German feeling).

By 1917 over **7 million** Russians had died. Retreating armies destroyed crops and buildings, creating millions of refugees. Industry was cut off from supplies, railway lines broke down, able-bodied men were sent to war, and **bread and flour** became scarce. Riots at bread shops were common by winter 1916.

steps.title: February Revolution 1917
steps.body:
- **22 February**: a lockout at a factory on the right bank; workers in 50 factories joined in sympathy.
- **23 February** (International Women's Day): women led strikes in many factories.
- **25 February**: the government suspended the Duma.
- **27 February**: soldiers, including cavalry, refused to fire and joined the strikers; the **Petrograd Soviet** was formed.
- **2 March**: the **Tsar abdicated**. Soviet leaders and Duma leaders formed a **Provisional Government**.
The February Revolution had no political party at its forefront; it was led by people themselves.

steps.title: October Revolution 1917
steps.body:
In **April 1917** Lenin returned from exile and put forward the **April Theses**: end the war, transfer land to peasants, nationalise banks. He also proposed renaming the Bolshevik Party the Communist Party.

The Provisional Government under **Kerenskii** grew weak. On **24 October 1917** a **Military Revolutionary Committee** of the Soviet, led by **Leon Trotsky**, seized government offices; the Winter Palace fell by night. A meeting of the All Russian Congress of Soviets approved the Bolshevik action. The (Julian-calendar) date explains why it is the October Revolution though it fell in November by today's calendar.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Name the three demands of the April Theses. (3 marks)**
1. Bring the war to a close. 2. Transfer land to the peasants. 3. Nationalise banks.

**Q2. How was the February Revolution different from October? (3 marks)**
- February: spontaneous, led by workers, women and soldiers; no single party; Tsar abdicated; Provisional Government formed.
- October: planned and led by the Bolshevik Party (Lenin, Trotsky); Provisional Government overthrown; Soviets took power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Tsar abdicated in the **February** Revolution, not October.
- Kerenskii headed the **Provisional Government**, not the Bolsheviks.
- Trotsky led the Military Revolutionary Committee; Lenin was the party leader.

activity.prompt: Order the events of 1917

events.text: Women lead strikes on International Women's Day
Lenin returns and gives the April Theses
Bolshevik uprising against the Provisional Government

quiz.q: St Petersburg was renamed during WWI as:
quiz.why: St Petersburg sounded German, so during the war with Germany it was renamed Petrograd. Leningrad came later after Lenin's death.

quiz.q: Which group did NOT lead the February Revolution?
quiz.why: The February Revolution was a spontaneous uprising of workers, women and soldiers; no single political party led it. So 'a single political party' is the group that did not lead it.

quiz.q: The April Theses were given by:
quiz.why: Lenin returned to Russia in April 1917 and put forward the April Theses, demanding an end to the war, transfer of land to peasants and nationalisation of banks.

quiz.q: Who headed the Provisional Government by October 1917?
quiz.why: After the Tsar fell, the Provisional Government ruled, and Kerenskii was its head by October 1917. Lenin led the Bolsheviks, who overthrew it.

quiz.q: The Military Revolutionary Committee in October 1917 was led by:
quiz.why: Leon Trotsky led the Military Revolutionary Committee, which organised the Bolshevik takeover in October 1917. Kerenskii led the government that was overthrown.

lessons.title: After October: civil war, collectivisation and global impact

scenes.text: 1929. Officials arrive at a village and tell well-off peasants (kulaks) to give up their land to a collective farm (kolkhoz).
Some peasants resist and slaughter their livestock. Grain production falls and a terrible famine follows.

steps.title: Changes after October
steps.body:
- Most industry and banks were **nationalised** (November 1917).
- Land was declared **social property**; peasants seized nobles' land.
- In cities, large houses were partitioned according to family needs; old aristocratic titles were banned; new uniforms were designed for the army and officials.
- The Bolshevik Party was renamed the **Russian Communist Party (Bolshevik)**.
- The **Constituent Assembly** elected in November 1917 was dismissed in **January 1918** when it did not support the Bolsheviks.
- In **March 1918** Russia made peace with Germany at **Brest-Litovsk**.
- A secret police (**Cheka**, later OGPU and NKVD) punished critics. Russia became a one-party state.

steps.title: Civil war and the USSR
steps.body: From 1918 to 1920 the Bolsheviks ('reds') fought non-Bolshevik socialists, liberals and supporters of autocracy ('greens' and 'whites'), who were backed by French, American, British and Japanese troops. The Bolsheviks largely won by January 1920. In **December 1922** the **USSR** was formed from the Russian Empire, granting political autonomy to most non-Russian nationalities, though unpopular policies alienated many.

steps.title: Planned economy and collectivisation
steps.body:
The Bolsheviks introduced **centralised planning**: officials set targets in **Five Year Plans** (the first two covered 1927–1932 and 1933–1938). Industrial production grew (oil, coal, steel) but work conditions were harsh.

Grain shortages led **Stalin** (who led after Lenin's death in 1924) to enforce **collectivisation from 1929**: peasants had to work on **collective farms (kolkhoz)**; profits were shared. **Kulaks** (well-off peasants) were raided and eliminated as a class. Resistance and livestock slaughter caused a fall in production and a devastating **famine (1930–33)** in which over 4 million died. Critics of the plan were deported or exiled.

steps.title: Global influence
steps.body: The Revolution inspired communist parties in many countries, including the **Communist Party of Great Britain**. The **Comintern** (Communist International), formed by the Bolsheviks, supported such parties. Many non-Russians, including Indians, attended the Communist University of the Workers of the East. By the 1950s it was clear the USSR had not lived up to its ideals: it was industrialised and offered education and health care, but denied essential freedoms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Collectivisation was **Stalin's** policy (from 1929), not Lenin's.
- 'Kulak' = well-off peasant, not a worker or a soldier.
- The USSR was formed in **1922**, not in 1917.

statements.s: The Bolsheviks dismissed the Constituent Assembly in January 1918.
statements.why: It did not support Bolshevik measures.

statements.s: Collectivisation was introduced by Lenin in 1917.
The USSR was formed in December 1922.
statements.why: It was created from the former Russian Empire.

statements.s: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk made peace with Germany.

quiz.q: Collective farms in the USSR were called:
quiz.why: After collectivisation, farms were merged into collective farms called kolkhoz, worked by peasants together. The Duma was a parliament, the Cheka secret police, and the Mir a village commune.

quiz.q: Kulaks were:
quiz.why: Kulaks were well-off peasants. Stalin blamed them for hoarding grain and targeted them during collectivisation. They were not factory owners or soldiers.

quiz.q: The Cheka was:
quiz.why: The Cheka was the Bolshevik secret police, set up to deal with opponents of the new state. It is not a newspaper or a parliament.

quiz.q: The famine following collectivisation occurred in:
quiz.why: The famine that followed collectivisation occurred in 1930–33 and killed millions. 1917–18 was the revolution period, and 1945 the end of the war.

quiz.q: The Comintern was:
options: An international union of pro-Bolshevik socialist parties
quiz.why: The Comintern, or Communist International, was an international union of socialist parties that supported the Bolsheviks. It was not a trade agreement or an army.

questions.q: Who led the Bolsheviks?
questions.why: Lenin led the Bolsheviks, who took power in October 1917. Kerenskii headed the Provisional Government, and Nicholas II was the Tsar.

questions.q: The Tsar of Russia in 1914 was:
questions.why: Nicholas II was the Tsar of Russia in 1914 and was overthrown in 1917. Alexander II, Peter I and Ivan IV ruled much earlier.

questions.q: Which party wanted nobles' land transferred to peasants?
questions.why: The Socialist Revolutionaries fought for the peasants and demanded that nobles' land be transferred to them. Liberals and conservatives did not support this.

questions.q: Which group believed only men of property should vote?
questions.why: Liberals wanted a nation tolerant of all religions but believed only men of property should vote. Radicals and socialists wanted wider voting rights.

questions.q: The Petrograd Soviet was formed during:
questions.why: The Petrograd Soviet was formed on 27 February 1917 during the February Revolution, when workers and soldiers set up a council. It was not part of 1905 or collectivisation.

questions.q: Who proposed government-supported cooperatives in France?
questions.why: Louis Blanc in France wanted the government to support cooperatives. Robert Owen set up cooperative communities privately, and Marx and Engels wanted a revolution.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The February Revolution was led by the Bolshevik Party. Reason (R): Lenin was in exile until April 1917.
questions.why: The assertion is false: no party led the February Revolution, and Bolsheviks did not lead it. The reason is true, since Lenin was in exile until April 1917, so only R is correct.

questions.q: Order: (i) USSR formed (ii) Bloody Sunday (iii) Brest-Litovsk (iv) collectivisation begins
questions.why: Chronological order: Bloody Sunday 1905, Brest-Litovsk 1918, USSR formed 1922, collectivisation began 1929. So the order is ii, iii, i, iv.

questions.q: Case: A factory owner in 1917 hears that banks will be nationalised and land will go to peasants. Which document announced these aims?
options: The Declaration of Rights of Man
questions.why: Lenin's April Theses announced nationalisation of banks, transfer of land to peasants and an end to the war. The Treaty of Versailles and Communist Manifesto are unrelated to those 1917 aims.

questions.q: Why did the Tsar's government lose support during WWI?
options: Huge casualties, food shortages and refusal to consult the Duma
questions.why: Russia's heavy casualties in the war (over 7 million), food shortages and the Tsar's refusal to consult the Duma made people turn against the government. A quick victory or booming industry would have helped him.

questions.q: If 7 million Russians died out of an army of 15 million mobilised, the share is about:
questions.why: Share = 7 ÷ 15 = 0.467, which is about 47%. Multiply by 100 to convert the fraction into a percentage.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Collectivisation led to a famine. Reason (R): Many peasants resisted and destroyed livestock, and production fell.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both statements are true. Peasants resisted collectivisation, destroyed livestock and production fell, which led to famine. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which statement about the Bolshevik state after 1918 is correct?
options: It became a one-party state with a secret police
questions.why: After 1918 the Bolsheviks formed a one-party state, with the Communist Party ruling alone and the Cheka punishing opponents. They did not restore the Tsar or allow many parties.

questions.q: Case: A historian says, 'The Revolution gave education and health care to millions but took away freedom of speech.' Which judgement does this match?
options: By the 1950s the USSR was industrialised but denied essential freedoms
The USSR was a liberal democracy
The USSR fully met its ideals
questions.why: The historian describes gains (education, health care) and losses (freedom of speech). That fits the balanced view that the USSR industrialised by the 1950s but denied essential freedoms.

questions.q: Why was the October Revolution so called though it occurred on 7 November by today's calendar?
options: It began in October and ended in November
Russia then followed the Julian calendar, 13 days behind the Gregorian
questions.why: Russia followed the Julian calendar until February 1918, which was 13 days behind the Gregorian calendar. So the revolution of 25 October (Julian) fell on 7 November in the modern calendar.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
courses.summary: How the Weimar Republic collapsed, how Hitler rose to power, what Nazi ideology preached, how it shaped youth and women, and why the Holocaust must be remembered.
outcomes: Learners can explain the problems of the Weimar Republic
Learners can describe how Hitler came to power and destroyed democracy
Learners can explain Nazi racial ideology and Lebensraum
Learners can describe the treatment of youth, women and minorities, and why remembrance matters
courses.guardianNote: This chapter discusses genocide (the Holocaust) and persecution in a factual, non-graphic way, as required by the Class 9 syllabus. The aim is understanding how hatred and propaganda work so that young people can recognise and reject them.

lessons.title: The birth and crises of the Weimar Republic

scenes.text: Berlin, 1923. Greta takes a basket of banknotes to buy a loaf of bread. By evening the price has risen again.
Her savings, enough for a house last year, now cannot buy a week's food.

steps.title: After the First World War
steps.body:
Imperial Germany was defeated in the First World War (1914–1918). The Kaiser abdicated and a **National Assembly met at Weimar** to create a democratic constitution with a federal structure. Deputies were elected to the **Reichstag** on the basis of equal and universal votes for all adults, including women.

The new **Weimar Republic** had to accept the harsh **Treaty of Versailles (1919)**: Germany lost its overseas colonies, a tenth of its population, 13% of its territory, 75% of its iron and 26% of its coal to France, Poland, Denmark and Lithuania. It was demilitarised, forced to accept a **War Guilt Clause**, and to pay **compensation of £6 billion**. The Allies occupied the resource-rich **Rhineland** for much of the 1920s.

steps.title: Economic crises
steps.body:
- Many Germans blamed the Republic for the defeat; its supporters were mockingly called the **'November criminals'**.
- In **1923** Germany refused to pay; France occupied the **Ruhr**, its leading industrial area. Germany printed paper money recklessly, causing **hyperinflation** — prices rose phenomenally high.
- The USA helped through the **Dawes Plan**, which reworked reparation terms.
- In **1929** the Wall Street Exchange crashed, starting the **Great Depression**. By **1932** German industrial production was reduced to **40%** of the 1929 level; up to 6 million were unemployed.

steps.title: Political weaknesses
steps.body:
The Weimar Constitution had defects that made it unstable:
- **Proportional representation** made it nearly impossible for one party to win a majority, so governments were coalitions.
- **Article 48** gave the President power to impose emergency, suspend civil rights and rule by decree.

Within its short life the Republic saw 20 different cabinets, lasting on average 239 days. People lost confidence in democracy.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why was the Treaty of Versailles resented? (3 marks)**
- Loss of colonies, territory, population and resources.
- War Guilt Clause blamed Germany alone; £6 billion compensation.
- Demilitarisation and occupation of the Rhineland hurt national pride.

**Q2. What was hyperinflation in Germany? (2 marks)**
In 1923, after Germany refused reparations and France occupied the Ruhr, Germany printed huge amounts of paper money; prices rose so fast that the mark became almost worthless.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Weimar Republic was **democratic**, not Nazi — it was named after the town where the Assembly met.
- The Dawes Plan was American help, not a German plan.
- Article 48 allowed **emergency rule by the President** — a weakness Hitler later exploited.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning
pairs: Harsh peace treaty imposed on Germany in 1919
Insult for supporters of the Republic

quiz.q: The Weimar Republic got its name from:
options: The town where the National Assembly met
quiz.why: The National Assembly met in the town of Weimar to set up a democratic constitution, so the new republic was called the Weimar Republic. It was not named after a leader or battle.

quiz.q: What share of its iron did Germany lose under the Treaty of Versailles?
quiz.why: Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany lost 75% of its iron ore, 26% of its coal and 13% of its territory. These losses crippled its economy.

quiz.q: Which area did France occupy in 1923?
quiz.why: In 1923 Germany could not pay reparations, so France occupied the Ruhr, Germany's leading industrial area, to claim coal. The Rhineland was a different region.

quiz.q: Proportional representation in Weimar Germany led to:
quiz.why: With proportional representation, seats are given by share of votes, so no party easily won a majority. This led to coalition governments, which were often unstable.

quiz.q: By 1932 industrial production in Germany was:
quiz.why: The Great Depression hit Germany hard, and by 1932 industrial production had fallen to about 40% of its 1929 level. Millions lost jobs.

lessons.title: Hitler's rise and the destruction of democracy

story.title: A speech in a beer hall

scenes.text: Hans, unemployed since 1930, hears a speaker promise jobs, a strong nation and an end to the 'injustice of Versailles'.
In 1932 he votes for the Nazi Party. Within a year, newspapers are censored and opponents disappear.

steps.title: Hitler's rise
steps.body:
**Adolf Hitler**, born in **1889** in Austria, fought in the German army in WWI. He joined a small group called the German Workers' Party and renamed it the **National Socialist German Workers' Party** — the **Nazi Party**.

In **1923** he planned to seize control of Bavaria and march to Berlin; he failed, was arrested and tried for treason, and later released. The Nazis gained mass support only after the **Great Depression**: in 1928 they got just 2.6% of votes; by **1932** they became the largest party with **37%** of votes.

Hitler was a powerful speaker. He promised to build a strong nation, undo Versailles, restore dignity, give jobs and secure a future for the youth. Nazi propaganda used rallies, red banners with the **swastika**, the Nazi salute and ritualised applause to project him as a messiah.

steps.title: Destroying democracy (1933 onwards)
steps.body:
- **30 January 1933**: President **Hindenburg** offered Hitler the Chancellorship.
- A mysterious **fire in the Reichstag (February 1933)**; the **Fire Decree of 28 February 1933** suspended civic rights like freedom of speech, press and assembly.
- Communists were sent to the first **concentration camps**.
- The **Enabling Act** (March 1933) established dictatorship: Hitler could rule by decree; all parties and trade unions except the Nazi Party were banned.
- Special forces: **SA (storm troopers)**, **Gestapo (secret state police)**, **SS (protection squads)**, criminal police and **SD (security service)** — with powers to detain people without legal procedures.

steps.title: Economy and foreign policy
steps.body:
Economist **Hjalmar Schacht** was given responsibility for recovery: state-funded work creation produced full production and employment, including the famous German superhighways and the people's car, the **Volkswagen**.

Foreign policy: Germany pulled out of the League of Nations in **1933**, reoccupied the Rhineland in **1936**, and integrated Austria (**1938**) under the slogan *One people, One empire, One leader*. It took the German-speaking **Sudetenland** from Czechoslovakia and then the whole country. In **September 1939** Germany invaded **Poland**, starting the Second World War. In **June 1941** it attacked the USSR. The USA entered after Japan bombed **Pearl Harbor** (December 1941). The war ended in **May 1945** with Hitler's defeat, and in August 1945 with the US atom bombing of Hiroshima.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did Nazism become popular by 1932? (3 marks)**
- The Depression caused unemployment and fear; people lost faith in the Weimar coalition governments.
- Hitler promised jobs, national pride and an end to Versailles.
- Skilful propaganda and mass rallies created a cult around him.

**Q2. How did Hitler destroy democracy? (3 marks)**
Fire Decree suspended civic rights → Enabling Act allowed rule by decree → all other parties and unions banned → security forces detained people without trial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hitler was **appointed** Chancellor by Hindenburg in 1933; he did not win an outright majority.
- WWII began with the invasion of **Poland** (1939), not the attack on the USSR.
- Gestapo = secret state police; SS = protection squads. Don't swap them.

activity.prompt: Put these events in order

events.text: Hyperinflation; Hitler's failed attempt in Bavaria

quiz.q: Who offered Hitler the Chancellorship?
quiz.why: President Hindenburg offered Hitler the Chancellorship on 30 January 1933 after Nazi support had grown. Goebbels and Himmler were Nazi leaders, not heads of state.

quiz.q: The Fire Decree suspended:
options: Civic rights like freedom of speech and press
quiz.why: The Fire Decree of February 1933 suspended civic rights such as freedom of speech, press and assembly, which had been guaranteed by the Weimar Constitution.

quiz.q: What share of votes did the Nazis get in 1932?
quiz.why: By 1932 the Nazis had become the largest party with 37% of the votes, up from 2.6% in 1928. The Great Depression was the chief reason.

quiz.q: Who led economic recovery under the Nazis?
quiz.why: Hjalmar Schacht was the economist who aimed for full production and full employment under the Nazis. Ebert and Hindenburg were presidents; Goebbels handled propaganda.

quiz.q: WWII began when Germany invaded:
quiz.why: Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 led Britain and France to declare war, starting the Second World War. Austria was joined to Germany without war in 1938.

lessons.title: Nazi ideology and the Holocaust

scenes.text: A Jewish family has lived in their town for generations. One day laws say they cannot be citizens or marry outside their group.
Years later, only one child survives. As an old woman she tells students: remember, and never let hatred grow quietly.

steps.title: Racial ideology
steps.body:
Nazi ideology was synonymous with Hitler's worldview. It claimed there was **no equality between people, only a racial hierarchy**: blond, blue-eyed **Nordic German Aryans** at the top and **Jews** at the lowest rung, called an 'anti-race'. All other coloured people were placed in between.

Hitler borrowed distorted ideas from **Charles Darwin** (natural selection) and **Herbert Spencer** ('survival of the fittest') — ideas they never intended for such use — to argue the strongest race would survive and others perish.

The idea of **Lebensraum (living space)**: new territories had to be acquired for settlement, to increase the area and resources of the mother country. Hence the push into Poland and the East.

steps.title: Steps of persecution
steps.body:
The Nazis wanted a society of 'pure and healthy Nordic Aryans'. Others were seen as 'undesirable': Germans considered impure or abnormal, **Jews, Gypsies (Roma), Blacks, Russians and Poles**.
- **1933–1938**: Jews were terrorised, pauperised and segregated. The **Nuremberg Laws (1935)** took away citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and Germans. Boycotts, expulsion from jobs, confiscation of property.
- **November 1938**: the **Kristallnacht** — a night of violence when Jewish homes, shops and synagogues were attacked.
- **1939–1945**: Jews were forced into **ghettos** and later killed in **gas chambers** in camps such as **Auschwitz** in occupied Poland. About six million Jews were killed in what is called the **Holocaust**.

steps.title: Why we remember
steps.body: After the war, the **Nuremberg Tribunal** prosecuted Nazi war criminals. Survivors' diaries (such as Anne Frank's), testimonies and memorials keep memory alive. The lesson for every generation: genocide does not begin with killing — it begins with propaganda, labelling a group as 'other', and ordinary people staying silent.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Explain Lebensraum. (2 marks)**
The Nazi idea that Germany needed new territories (especially in the East) for settlement, to increase its area and resources.

**Q2. Describe the stages of Nazi persecution of Jews. (3 marks)**
Step 1 (1933–38): exclusion — Nuremberg Laws, boycotts, loss of jobs and property. Step 2: violence — Kristallnacht 1938. Step 3 (1939–45): ghettoisation and mass killing in gas chambers — the Holocaust.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Darwin and Spencer did **not** advocate Nazi racism — the Nazis misused their ideas.
- 'Aryan' as used by the Nazis was a pseudo-scientific myth, not a real biological race.
- The Holocaust targeted Jews above all, but Roma, disabled people, Poles and others were also persecuted.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of Nazi persecution
items: Propaganda labels Jews as an 'anti-race'
Nuremberg Laws remove citizenship (1935)
Kristallnacht violence (1938)
Jews forced into ghettos
Mass killing in gas chambers (Holocaust)

quiz.q: Who were at the top of the Nazi racial hierarchy?
quiz.why: The Nazi racial hierarchy placed Nordic German Aryans at the top, with Jews, Gypsies and others at the bottom. Slavs were also treated as inferior.

quiz.q: Lebensraum means:
quiz.why: Lebensraum means 'living space'. Hitler wanted to acquire more territory for Germany by conquest, especially in the east. Blitzkrieg means lightning war.

quiz.q: The Nuremberg Laws (1935):
options: Took citizenship away from Jews and banned intermarriage
quiz.why: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 took citizenship from Jews and banned marriage between Jews and Germans, making exclusion legal. They did not give any rights.

quiz.q: Auschwitz was:
options: A killing centre in occupied Poland
quiz.why: Auschwitz was a camp in occupied Poland where the Nazis carried out mass killings, mostly of Jews. It was not a treaty, newspaper or ordinary city.

quiz.q: Which thinkers' ideas did the Nazis distort?
quiz.why: Nazi ideas of race misused Darwin's theory of natural selection and Spencer's phrase 'survival of the fittest' to claim some races were superior. Locke, Rousseau and Marx are not tied to this.

lessons.title: Youth, women, propaganda and ordinary people

scenes.text: At 10, Karl joins the Jungvolk; at 14 he must join the Hitler Youth. His textbooks praise war and blame Jews.
At the cinema a film shows minorities as rats. His grandmother quietly says, 'They want you to hate before you think.'

steps.title: Youth in Nazi Germany
steps.body:
Hitler believed a strong Nazi society required children taught Nazi ideology.
- Schools were 'cleansed': Jewish and 'politically unreliable' teachers dismissed; children segregated (Germans and Jews could not sit together).
- Textbooks were rewritten; **racial science** was introduced to justify Nazi ideas of race; sport aimed at violence and aggression.
- Youth organisations: at **10** children entered **Jungvolk**; at **14** all boys joined the **Hitler Youth**, then labour service at 18, then the army.
- The Youth League was founded in 1922 and renamed Hitler Youth four years later.

steps.title: The 'Nazi cult of motherhood'
steps.body: Girls were told to become good mothers and rear pure-blooded Aryan children, maintain racial purity and teach Nazi values. Women who bore racially 'desirable' children were rewarded: hospital privileges, shop and travel concessions; **Honour Crosses** — **bronze for four children, silver for six, gold for eight or more**. Women who married 'undesired' groups were publicly punished.

steps.title: The art of propaganda
steps.body:
The Nazis used careful words: they never said 'kill' — they used terms like 'special treatment', 'final solution' (for Jews), 'euthanasia' (for the disabled), 'evacuation'. Media — films, radio, posters, slogans and leaflets — were used to win support. Propaganda minister **Goebbels** oversaw this; films like *The Eternal Jew* spread hatred.

Ordinary people: many saw the world through Nazi eyes; some resisted (the **Bonhoeffer**-type pastors, student groups), but most remained **passive onlookers**. Pastor **Martin Niemoeller** later reflected that because he did not speak up when others were taken, there was no one left to speak for him.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What were the Honour Crosses? (2 marks)**
Awards to German mothers of 'desirable' children: bronze for 4, silver for 6, gold for 8 or more children.

**Q2. How did the Nazis use language as propaganda? (3 marks)**
They hid mass killing behind soft terms ('special treatment', 'final solution', 'evacuation'), depicted Jews through stereotypes in films and posters, and ran an organised ministry under Goebbels to shape public opinion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Boys joined the Hitler Youth at **14**, not 10 (10 = Jungvolk).
- Gold Honour Cross = **8 or more** children, not 4.
- Do not use propaganda terms like 'final solution' without explaining that they hid mass murder.

steps.title: Lessons for today
steps.body: Ask of any message you see online: Who made it? Who does it blame? Does it treat a group as less human? Hate propaganda depends on silent bystanders — reporting, questioning and speaking up matter.

a.text: In your class WhatsApp group, someone shares a meme mocking a religious community as 'dirty'. Several people laugh.

choices.label: Laugh along so you fit in
choices.feedback: This is how bystanders let hate grow.

choices.label: Say politely it isn't okay to mock a whole community
choices.feedback: Speaking up breaks the chain of hate.

b.text: More memes follow, getting worse. A classmate from that community leaves the group in tears.

choices.label: Message her privately and tell a teacher
choices.feedback: It's never too late to act.

c.text: You remember the lesson of Nazi propaganda: hatred starts with labels and silence. Speaking up protects everyone.

quiz.q: At what age did children join the Jungvolk?
quiz.why: Children joined the Jungvolk at age 10 and the Hitler Youth at 14. The order of the ages matches the Nazi youth organisation system.

quiz.q: A gold Honour Cross was given to mothers of:
quiz.why: Under the Nazi policy, mothers received a bronze cross for four children, silver for six and gold for eight or more. It encouraged 'Aryan' mothers to have many children.

quiz.q: Who was the Nazi propaganda minister?
quiz.why: Joseph Goebbels was the Nazi minister of propaganda, who controlled media and public opinion. Schacht was an economist and Niemoeller a pastor.

quiz.q: 'Racial science' was introduced in Nazi schools to:
quiz.why: 'Racial science' in Nazi schools was pseudo-science meant to justify Nazi ideas of race and Aryan superiority. It was not real genetics.

quiz.q: Why are euphemisms like 'evacuation' important to understand?
options: They were polite words for travel
quiz.why: Nazis used words like 'evacuation', 'special treatment' and 'final solution' to hide that people were being killed. Understanding this helps us see how language can disguise mass murder.

questions.q: Nazi stands for:
questions.why: Nazi is short for the National Socialist German Workers' Party, the party Hitler led. The other options are invented.

questions.q: Hitler was born in:
questions.why: Hitler was born in Austria in 1889. He later moved to Germany and became its leader in 1933.

questions.q: The swastika was used by the Nazis as:
questions.why: The Nazis used the swastika as a party symbol on their banners and in propaganda. It was not a coin, treaty or law.

questions.q: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in:
questions.why: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919, after the First Ended in 1918. It placed harsh terms on Germany.

questions.q: The Gestapo was:
questions.why: The Gestapo was the Nazi secret state police that arrested and tortured opponents. The Storm Troopers and Hitler Youth were different Nazi groups.

questions.q: Which treaty demand hurt Germany's pride most directly?
questions.why: The War Guilt Clause blamed Germany alone for the war, hurting its pride and forcing it to pay reparations. The Fire Decree and Enabling Act were Nazi measures, and the Dawes Plan eased payments.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Weimar governments were often coalitions. Reason (R): Proportional representation made a single-party majority hard.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Proportional representation divided votes among many parties, so a single party rarely got a majority, forcing coalitions. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: In 1936 German troops re-enter a western region that the Allies had demilitarised. This is:
questions.why: In 1936 Hitler sent troops into the Rhineland, a demilitarised area on Germany's western border, breaking the Versailles Treaty. The Ruhr was occupied by France in 1923.

questions.q: Which came LAST?
questions.why: The Nuremberg Laws were in 1935, Kristallnacht in 1938, the invasion of Poland in 1939 and the attack on the USSR in June 1941, so the attack on the USSR came last.

questions.q: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution:
options: Gave the President emergency powers to rule by decree
questions.why: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution let the President suspend civic rights and rule by decree in an emergency. This weakness was later used to suspend rights.

questions.q: If prices doubled every week for 4 weeks, a loaf costing 1 mark would cost:
questions.why: Doubling each week for 4 weeks gives 1 × 2⁴ = 16 marks. The price goes 2, 4, 8, 16. This shows how fast hyperinflation grows.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Nazis won wide support after 1929. Reason (R): The Great Depression caused mass unemployment and loss of faith in Weimar.
questions.why: Both statements are true. The Depression brought mass unemployment and people lost faith in the Weimar Republic, so they turned to the Nazis. Their vote rose from 2.6% to 37%.

questions.q: Which measure finally established dictatorship legally?
questions.why: The Enabling Act of March 1933 gave Hitler the power to rule by decree and ban other parties, legally establishing his dictatorship. The Fire Decree only suspended rights.

questions.q: Case: A pastor says after the war, 'When they came for others I did not speak; when they came for me, no one was left.' What does this teach?
questions.why: Niemoeller's words show that when people stay silent as others are persecuted, they can later be victims too. It teaches that silence by bystanders helped the persecution.

questions.q: Why did the USA enter WWII?
options: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941
questions.why: The USA entered the war after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Germany invaded Poland in 1939 and the USSR in 1941, but these did not directly bring in the USA.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Forest Society and Colonialism
courses.note: Some boards treat this chapter as internal-assessment only; content is complete for study.
courses.summary: Why colonial rule cleared forests, how forest laws and scientific forestry changed forest people's lives, and the rebellions of Bastar and Java.
outcomes: Learners can explain causes of deforestation under colonial rule
Learners can describe the forest acts and scientific forestry
Learners can explain the effects on shifting cultivators, nomads and traders
Learners can compare the Bastar rebellion and the Samin movement in Java

lessons.title: Why forests disappeared

story.title: The sal tree and the railway

scenes.text: 1870s. Villagers watch British contractors cut a huge sal forest that gave them fruit, leaves and medicine.
The logs become railway sleepers. A forest that took centuries to grow vanishes in a few seasons.

steps.title: Land to be improved
steps.body:
Deforestation means the disappearance of forests. Under colonial rule it became systematic.

**Expansion of cultivation**: as population grew and food demand rose, peasants extended cultivation. The British encouraged commercial crops — **jute, sugar, wheat and cotton** — for growing European populations and for factories. Colonial officials thought forests were unproductive and wild land that had to be brought under cultivation to produce revenue. Between **1880 and 1920**, cultivated area rose by about **6.7 million hectares**.

steps.title: Sleepers on the tracks and ship-building
steps.body:
- By the early 19th century oak forests in England were disappearing, creating a timber shortage for the **Royal Navy**. Search parties explored Indian forests; within a decade trees were felled on a massive scale and exported.
- **Railways** (from the 1850s) needed wood as fuel for locomotives and for **sleepers** to hold the tracks. Each mile of track required between **1,760 and 2,000 sleepers**.
- **Plantations**: large areas of natural forest were cleared for **tea, coffee and rubber** to meet Europe's demand. Land was given to Europeans at cheap rates.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the British consider forests 'unproductive'? (2 marks)**
Forests yielded no agricultural produce or land revenue, so the British saw them as wilderness to be cleared for crops that brought revenue.

**Q2. How did railways cause deforestation? (3 marks)**
Step 1: locomotives needed wood as fuel. Step 2: tracks needed sleepers — 1,760–2,000 per mile. Step 3: the government gave contracts to individuals who cut trees indiscriminately, and forests around railway tracks disappeared fast.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deforestation was not only due to railways — cultivation, ship-building and plantations mattered too.
- Don't write 'sleepers' as beds for workers — they are the wooden beams under rails.

activity.prompt: Which cause of deforestation is described?

items.text: Demand for jute, cotton and wheat
Oak shortage for the Royal Navy

quiz.q: Deforestation means:
quiz.why: Deforestation is the disappearance of forests as trees are cut down and land is cleared. Planting forests is the opposite, called afforestation.

quiz.q: How many sleepers did one mile of railway track need?
quiz.why: Each mile of railway track needed about 1,760 to 2,000 sleepers, so railway expansion used huge numbers of trees.

quiz.q: Between 1880 and 1920, cultivated area rose by about:
quiz.why: Between 1880 and 1920 the cultivated area in India rose by about 6.7 million hectares as forests were cleared for farming.

quiz.q: England needed Indian timber partly because:
quiz.why: By the early 1800s oak forests in England were disappearing, which threatened timber supply for the Royal Navy's ships. So England looked to India for timber.

quiz.q: Plantations were cleared for:
quiz.why: Large forest areas were cleared for plantations of tea, coffee and rubber to meet European demand. They were not mainly for rice, wheat or jute.

lessons.title: The rise of commercial forestry and forest laws

scenes.text: A village woman goes to collect firewood as her mother did. A forest guard stops her: 'This is a reserved forest now.'
She is fined. To use the forest, families must now bribe guards with gifts of food.

steps.title: Brandis and scientific forestry
steps.body:
The British called in a German expert, **Dietrich Brandis**, and made him the first **Inspector General of Forests** in India. He set up the **Indian Forest Service in 1864** and helped formulate the **Indian Forest Act of 1865**. The **Imperial Forest Research Institute** was set up at **Dehradun in 1906**.

**Scientific forestry**: natural forests with many kinds of trees were cut down and replaced by **one type of tree planted in straight rows** — a **plantation**. Forest officials surveyed, estimated the area under each tree type and made working plans for how much to cut and replant.

steps.title: The Forest Acts
steps.body:
The 1865 Act was amended twice — in **1878** and **1927**. The 1878 Act divided forests into three categories:
- **Reserved** — best forests; villagers could not take anything, even for their own use.
- **Protected**
- **Village forests**
For house building or fuel, villagers could take wood only from protected or village forests.

steps.title: How lives were affected
steps.body:
- Everyday practices — cutting wood, grazing cattle, collecting fruits and roots, hunting and fishing — became **illegal**. People were forced to steal wood and were at the mercy of forest guards who demanded bribes.
- **Shifting cultivation** (also called **swidden**; in India 'dhya', 'penda', 'bewar', 'nevad', 'jhum', 'podu', 'khandad', 'kumri') was banned: Europeans thought it harmful to forests, a fire risk and hard to tax. Many communities were forcibly displaced.
- **Hunting** for food was banned for villagers, but hunting big game became sport for the colonial elite; rewards were given for killing tigers and wolves; over **80,000 tigers, 150,000 leopards and 200,000 wolves** were killed between 1875 and 1925.
- **Trade**: the British gave large European trading firms the sole right to trade in forest products; some communities like the Korava, Karacha and Yerukula of Madras Presidency were branded 'criminal tribes'. Many were forced to work in factories, mines and plantations, including **tea plantations in Assam**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the British ban shifting cultivation? (3 marks)**
- They felt land used for a few years and then abandoned could not grow trees for railway timber.
- Burning the forest risked spreading fires that destroyed valuable timber.
- It made calculating and collecting taxes difficult.

**Q2. What is scientific forestry? (2 marks)**
Replacing mixed natural forests with single-species plantations in straight rows, managed by working plans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Brandis was **German**, not British.
- Reserved forests were the *most* restricted; villagers could take wood from protected/village forests only.
- 'Scientific' forestry was not ecologically better — it reduced diversity.

activity.prompt: Match the item

quiz.q: The Indian Forest Service was set up in:
quiz.why: The Indian Forest Service was set up in 1864 with Dietrich Brandis, a German expert, as its first Inspector General.

quiz.q: The Forest Act was amended in:
quiz.why: The Forest Act was first passed in 1865 and amended in 1878 and 1927. The 1878 amendment divided forests into three categories.

quiz.q: Under the 1878 Act, the best forests were:
quiz.why: The 1878 Act divided forests into reserved, protected and village forests. The best forests were called reserved forests, and villagers could not take anything from them.

quiz.q: 'Jhum' is a name for:
quiz.why: Jhum is the name used in north-east India for shifting cultivation, in which land is cleared and burnt, then left fallow. It is not a tree or a tax.

quiz.q: Where was the Imperial Forest Research Institute set up?
quiz.why: The Imperial Forest Research Institute was set up in Dehradun in 1906, to train forest officers and study scientific forestry.

lessons.title: Rebellion in the forest: Bastar, 1910

story.title: Mango boughs and lumps of earth

scenes.text: 1910, Bastar. Villagers pass mango boughs, a lump of earth, chillies and arrows from village to village.
It is a message: rise against the British. Markets are looted, police stations burnt.

steps.title: The people of Bastar
steps.body:
**Bastar** lies in the southernmost part of present-day **Chhattisgarh**, bordering Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Maharashtra. The **Indrawati** river flows across it east to west.

It is home to communities such as **Maria and Muria Gonds, Dhurwas, Bhatras and Halbas**. They believed each village was given its land by the Earth, and made offerings to the earth at each agricultural festival. They respected the spirits of the river, forest and mountain. If people from one village wanted wood from another village's forest, they paid a small fee called **devsari, dand or man**.

steps.title: Causes and course of the rebellion
steps.body:
- In **1905** the colonial government proposed to **reserve two-thirds** of the forest, stop shifting cultivation, hunting and collection of forest produce.
- Some villages were allowed to stay in reserved forests on condition they worked free for the forest department ('forest villages').
- People suffered from increased land rents and frequent demands for free labour and goods by officials; terrible famines in **1899–1900** and **1907–1908**.
- The **Dhurwas** of the Kanger forest, where reservation first happened, took the lead. **Gunda Dhur**, from village Nethanar, is said to be an important leader.
- In 1910 messages were passed using mango boughs, earth, chillies and arrows; bazaars were looted, officials' houses, schools and police stations were burnt and robbed.
- The British sent troops to suppress it. It took three months to regain control. A victory for the rebels: work on reservation was **temporarily suspended** and the area to be reserved was reduced to roughly **half**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the people of Bastar rebel in 1910? (3 marks)**
- Proposal (1905) to reserve two-thirds of forests, ban shifting cultivation and forest produce.
- Forced labour in 'forest villages' and higher rents.
- Famines of 1899–1900 and 1907–08 deepened distress.

**Q2. What was the outcome? (2 marks)**
The British suppressed it in three months, but reservation was suspended and the reserved area reduced to about half.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Bastar is in **Chhattisgarh** (it was in a princely state before independence), not Jharkhand.
- The rebellion was **in 1910**; the reservation proposal was in **1905**.
- Gunda Dhur was of the **Dhurwa** community, not a British official.

statements.s: Bastar is in present-day Chhattisgarh.
The rebellion led to the reserved area being reduced to about half.
statements.why: Work was suspended and area reduced.
