lessons.title: Lakes, rivers and the economy, and river pollution

scenes.text: Ishaan sees white foam on a river near a factory town.
His school joins a riverside clean-up and learns how sewage, industrial waste and plastics choke rivers.

steps.title: Lakes of India
steps.body:
Most lakes are **permanent**; some contain water only in rainy season. Types:
- **Freshwater** lakes mostly in the Himalayas, many of glacial origin: **Wular** (J&K — formed by tectonic activity; **largest freshwater lake**), **Dal, Bhimtal, Nainital, Loktak** (Manipur), **Barapani** (Meghalaya).
- **Ox-bow lakes** form when a meandering river cuts off a loop.
- **Lagoons** in coastal areas: **Chilika, Pulicat, Kolleru**.
- **Salt lakes** in inland drainage areas: **Sambhar** (Rajasthan) — its water is used to produce salt.
- **Man-made lakes** formed by damming rivers for hydel power, e.g. Guru Gobind Sagar (Bhakra-Nangal).

steps.title: Rivers, the economy and pollution
steps.body:
Rivers give water for irrigation, navigation and hydroelectricity, and have attracted settlements since ancient times; many cities stand on river banks.

Lakes help regulate the flow of rivers, prevent flooding, maintain flow during dry seasons, moderate climate, support aquatic life, and add to tourism.

Growing domestic, municipal, industrial and agricultural demand for water reduces flow and adds pollution: **untreated sewage and industrial effluents** are dumped into rivers. River-cleaning programmes such as the **Ganga Action Plan (1985)**, later the **National River Conservation Plan**, and the **Namami Gange** mission aim to treat sewage and restore rivers.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Give three uses of lakes. (3 marks)**
Regulate river flow and prevent floods; supply water in dry seasons and for hydel power; moderate climate, maintain ecosystems and support tourism.

**Q2. How are rivers polluted and what can citizens do? (3 marks)**
Causes: sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural chemicals, solid waste. Actions: not dumping waste/plastic, supporting sewage treatment, reporting industrial discharge, joining clean-up drives.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wular is **freshwater** (largest); Chilika is **saltwater** lagoon; Sambhar is a **salt lake**.
- Ox-bow lakes form from **meanders**, not from glaciers.

activity.prompt: Classify each lake

quiz.q: Largest freshwater lake in India:
quiz.why: Wular lake in Jammu and Kashmir is the largest freshwater lake in India. Chilika is a saltwater lagoon, and Dal and Loktak are smaller freshwater lakes.

quiz.q: Sambhar lake is used for:
quiz.why: Sambhar is a salt lake in Rajasthan, and its water is used to produce salt. It is not mainly used for power, navigation or fishing.

quiz.q: Loktak lake is in:
quiz.why: Loktak lake lies in Manipur. It is a freshwater lake famous for its floating vegetation.

quiz.q: Ox-bow lakes form from:
quiz.why: Ox-bow lakes form when a meandering river cuts off a loop in its course, leaving a crescent-shaped lake. Volcanoes, glaciers and coral form other types.

quiz.q: The Ganga Action Plan was launched in:
quiz.why: The Ganga Action Plan was launched in 1985 to reduce pollution in the Ganga. 2005 and 1960 are not its launch dates.

questions.q: Which river is called the 'sorrow of Bihar'?
questions.why: The Kosi is called the 'sorrow of Bihar' because it often floods and changes course, causing damage. The Son, Gandak and Ghaghara are other rivers.

questions.q: The largest peninsular river:
questions.why: The Godavari is the largest river of peninsular India, about 1,500 km long. The Krishna and Kaveri are shorter, and the Narmada flows west.

questions.q: Chilika is a:
questions.why: Chilika is a saltwater lagoon on the Odisha coast, separated from the sea by a sandbar. It is not a dam or glacier.

questions.q: The Indus Water Treaty was signed in:
questions.why: The Indus Water Treaty between India and Pakistan was signed in 1960, sharing the waters of the Indus system. 1947 was Independence, and 1985 the Ganga Action Plan.

questions.q: The Yamuna joins the Ganga at:
questions.why: The Yamuna joins the Ganga at Prayagraj (Allahabad). Patna and Haridwar lie on the Ganga but the Yamuna does not meet it there.

questions.q: Which river flows through a rift valley?
questions.why: The Narmada flows through a rift valley, a long trough between faults, as does the Tapi. The Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna flow through other landscapes.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Peninsular rivers are mostly seasonal. Reason (R): They depend mainly on monsoon rainfall.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Peninsular rivers do not get snow-melt, and rely mainly on the monsoon rains, so their flow varies by season. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A river makes a U-turn at Namcha Barwa and enters India through a gorge. Name it in Arunachal.
questions.why: The Brahmaputra makes a U-turn at Namcha Barwa and enters India through a gorge in Arunachal Pradesh, where it is called the Dihang. The Subansiri and Lohit are its tributaries.

questions.q: Which is NOT a tributary of the Krishna?
questions.why: The Wainganga is a tributary of the Godavari, not the Krishna. Bhima, Koyana and Tungabhadra join the Krishna.

questions.q: Which is correct about the Sundarban delta?
questions.why: The Sundarban delta, formed by the Ganga and Brahmaputra, is the world's largest and fastest-growing delta. It is on the Bay of Bengal, not the Arabian Sea.

questions.q: If the Indus system carries 100 units of water, how many units can India use under the 1960 treaty?
questions.why: Under the 1960 treaty India can use about 20% of the water of the Indus system, so out of 100 units, 20. The remaining 80% goes to Pakistan.

questions.q: Combined length of Godavari (1,500 km) and Krishna (1,400 km) exceeds the Indus (2,900 km) by:
questions.why: 1,500 + 1,400 = 2,900 km, which equals the Indus's length, so the difference is 0 km. Add first, then compare.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Brahmaputra carries more silt in Assam than in Tibet. Reason (R): Tibet is cold and dry while Assam gets heavy rainfall.
questions.why: Both statements are true. Tibet is cold and dry, so the river carries little silt there, but heavy rainfall in Assam adds water and silt. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A town wants to reduce floods and also store water for the dry season. Which natural feature helps both?
questions.why: Lakes help regulate river flow during floods and store water for the dry season. Glaciers melting faster would raise floods, and dunes and deserts store no water.

questions.q: Why do west-flowing Narmada and Tapi lack deltas while east-flowing rivers have them?
options: They flow fast through rift valleys into the sea, forming estuaries
questions.why: The Narmada and Tapi flow quickly through narrow rift valleys, with little room to deposit sediment, so they form estuaries, not deltas. East-flowing rivers slow down on broad plains.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Climate
courses.summary: What controls India's climate, how the monsoon works, the four seasons, rainfall distribution, and why the monsoon unites India.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish weather and climate and list climatic controls
Learners can explain the mechanism of the monsoon
Learners can describe the four seasons with local phenomena
Learners can explain rainfall distribution and the monsoon as a unifying bond

lessons.title: Weather, climate and climatic controls

scenes.text: In December, Aisha in Drass (Ladakh) faces temperatures far below freezing.
Her pen-friend in Thiruvananthapuram writes that it is warm and humid there.

steps.title: Weather vs climate
steps.body:
**Weather** is the state of the atmosphere over an area at a point of time. **Climate** is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for a long period (more than **thirty years**). Elements: temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation.

India's climate is the **monsoon type** (found mainly in south and south-east Asia). The word **monsoon** comes from the Arabic **'mausim'** meaning season — a seasonal reversal in wind direction.

steps.title: Six climatic controls
steps.body:
1. **Latitude** – the Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle; the south is tropical, the north subtropical.
2. **Altitude** – temperature falls with height; the Himalayas (avg 6,000 m) block cold Central Asian winds.
3. **Pressure and winds** – depend on latitude and altitude.
4. **Distance from the sea** – coastal areas have moderate (maritime) climate; interior areas have extreme (**continentality**).
5. **Ocean currents** – with onshore winds affect coastal climate.
6. **Relief** – high mountains block winds and cause rain on the windward side (orographic rain); leeward side stays dry.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why do coastal areas have less temperature range than interiors? (2 marks)**
The sea moderates temperature (land heats and cools faster than water), so coastal places experience little difference between summer and winter.

**Q2. How does the Himalaya influence India's climate? (2 marks)**
It blocks cold winds from Central Asia, keeping winters milder, and traps monsoon winds, forcing them to shed moisture in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Weather = short-term; climate = long-term (30+ years). Don't swap.
- 'Mausim' (Arabic) means **season**, not rain.

activity.prompt: Weather or climate?

items.text: It is raining in Pune this afternoon
Rajasthan receives low rainfall every year
Today's maximum temperature in Delhi is 38°C
Kerala has a hot, humid tropical climate

quiz.q: Climate is studied over a period of at least:
quiz.why: Climate is the average weather of a place studied over a long period, usually over 30 years. A single year only shows the weather.

quiz.q: 'Monsoon' comes from 'mausim' meaning:
quiz.why: 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic word 'mausim', which means season, referring to the seasonal reversal of winds.

quiz.q: Continentality causes:
quiz.why: Continentality means places far from the sea have extreme temperatures, with hot summers and cold winters. Coastal places are moderate because of the sea.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a climatic control?
quiz.why: Latitude, altitude, relief and distance from the sea are climatic controls. Population does not decide a place's climate.

quiz.q: Rain on the windward side of mountains is called:
quiz.why: Rain caused by moist air forced up the windward side of a mountain is called orographic or relief rain. Convectional rain comes from heating and cyclonic rain from storms.

lessons.title: Factors affecting India's climate and the monsoon mechanism

scenes.text: An old fisherman in Kerala watches the sea turn rough in late May and the wind blow steadily from the south-west.
'The monsoon is coming,' he says. A few days later, the burst of the monsoon drenches the coast.

steps.title: Pressure, winds and jet streams
steps.body:
- In winter, a high-pressure area lies north of the Himalayas; cold dry winds blow from this region to the low-pressure areas over the oceans to the south.
- In summer, a low-pressure area develops over interior Asia and north-western India; winds reverse and blow from the high-pressure southern Indian Ocean towards the land, crossing the equator and turning right (**Coriolis force**) — the **south-west monsoon**.
- **Jet streams**: narrow belts of high-altitude (above 12,000 m) westerly winds. The **sub-tropical westerly jet stream** lies south of the Himalayas in winter; in summer it shifts north and an **easterly jet stream** blows over peninsular India.
- **Western cyclonic disturbances** from the Mediterranean bring winter rain to the north-western plains.

steps.title: Mechanism of the monsoon
steps.body:
1. **Differential heating and cooling** of land and water creates low pressure on the Indian landmass and high pressure over the seas.
2. Shift of the **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** in summer over the Ganga plain (the **monsoon trough**).
3. A high-pressure area east of **Madagascar** (about 20°S) affects the monsoon.
4. The **Tibetan plateau** gets intensely heated in summer, creating strong vertical air currents and low pressure.
5. Movement of the westerly jet stream north of the Himalayas and the tropical easterly jet over the peninsula.
6. **Southern Oscillation**: pressure changes between the Indian and Pacific Oceans; **El Niño**, a warm ocean current off Peru in some years, is linked to weaker Indian monsoons. The **ENSO** combination is used for long-range forecasting.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What is 'break' in the monsoon? (2 marks)** Wet and dry spells: the monsoon rains for a few days, then has rainless intervals, linked to movement of the monsoon trough.

**Q2. Explain the role of differential heating. (3 marks)** In summer, land heats faster than sea → low pressure over land, high over sea → moisture-laden winds blow from sea to land → rain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The south-east trade winds **become** the south-west monsoon after crossing the equator (deflected by Coriolis force).
- El Niño is a **warm** current linked to **weaker** Indian monsoons, not stronger.
- Western disturbances bring **winter** rain to the north-west, not summer rain.

activity.prompt: Order the summer monsoon process
items: Land heats faster than the sea in summer
Low pressure forms over north-west India and Tibet
ITCZ shifts north over the Ganga plain
Trade winds from the southern ocean cross the equator
Coriolis force turns them into south-west winds
Moist winds bring rain to India

quiz.q: ITCZ stands for:
quiz.why: ITCZ stands for Inter Tropical Convergence Zone, a low-pressure belt near the equator where trade winds meet. Its shift north in summer helps bring the monsoon.

quiz.q: El Niño is a:
quiz.why: El Niño is a warm ocean current that appears off the coast of Peru every few years. It affects weather and is linked with weak monsoons in India.

quiz.q: Winter rain in Punjab is caused by:
quiz.why: Winter rain in Punjab and nearby areas is caused by western cyclonic disturbances from the Mediterranean region. The south-west monsoon is the summer rain.

quiz.q: Jet streams blow at heights above:
quiz.why: Jet streams are fast narrow wind currents in the upper atmosphere, blowing at heights above about 12,000 m. They are well above the surface winds.

quiz.q: The force that deflects winds to the right in the northern hemisphere:
quiz.why: The Coriolis force, caused by the Earth's rotation, deflects winds to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern.

lessons.title: The four seasons of India

scenes.text: January: Delhi fog delays Vivek's train. February: rain from a western disturbance helps the wheat crop.
May: the loo blows. June: the monsoon bursts. October: it is hot and humid — the 'October heat'.

steps.title: Cold weather season (winter)
steps.body: From **mid-November to February**; December and January are the coldest in north India. Temperature decreases from south to north (Chennai ~24–25°C; northern plains 10–15°C). Days warm, nights cold; frost common in the north; higher slopes of the Himalayas get snowfall. North-east trade winds prevail; they blow from land to sea, so most of India has a **dry season**, but **Tamil Nadu coast gets rain** (winds blow from sea to land there). Western cyclonic disturbances bring winter rain to the plains — locally called **'mahawat'** — vital for **rabi** crops.

steps.title: Hot weather season (summer)
steps.body: From **March to May**; the heat belt shifts north as the sun's apparent movement shifts. In May temperatures of **45°C** are common in north-west India. Hot, dry winds called **'loo'** blow over north and north-west India in the afternoon. Dust storms are common in May. Local thunderstorms: **'kaal baisakhi'** in **West Bengal** (calamity of the month of Baisakh). Pre-monsoon showers in **Kerala and Karnataka** help the early ripening of mangoes — **'mango showers'**.

steps.title: Advancing and retreating monsoon
steps.body:
**Advancing monsoon (rainy season)**: begins early **June**; the monsoon arrives on the Kerala coast around **1 June** with a sudden onset — the **'burst'** — and covers the country by early to mid-July. Two branches: **Arabian Sea branch** and **Bay of Bengal branch**. **Mawsynram** (Khasi hills, Meghalaya) receives the highest average rainfall in the world. Breaks in monsoon occur.

**Retreating monsoon (transition)**: **October–November**. Low-pressure trough weakens; monsoon withdraws; skies clear, temperature rises; high humidity makes weather oppressive — **'October heat'**. In early November low-pressure conditions move to the Bay of Bengal, causing **cyclonic depressions**; the **Coromandel coast** gets much of its rain during this time; deltas of Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri are often struck by cyclones.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why does the Tamil Nadu coast get rain in winter? (2 marks)** North-east trade winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and blow from sea to land there.

**Q2. What is 'October heat'? (2 marks)** After the monsoon retreats, clear skies and rising temperature combined with high ground moisture make the weather hot and humid in October.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mango showers = **Kerala/Karnataka**; kaal baisakhi = **West Bengal**. Don't swap.
- Mawsynram (not Cherrapunji) gets the world's **highest average** rainfall.
- The retreating monsoon is in **Oct–Nov**, not Aug–Sep.

activity.prompt: Match the local phenomenon
pairs: Hot dry winds in north India, summer
Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka
Hot humid weather after monsoon retreat

quiz.q: The monsoon reaches Kerala around:
quiz.why: The south-west monsoon normally reaches the Kerala coast around 1 June. It then spreads over most of India by mid-July.

quiz.q: Which place gets the highest average rainfall in the world?
quiz.why: Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives the highest average rainfall in the world. Cherrapunji is close by and also very wet, but Mawsynram is higher.

quiz.q: Kaal baisakhi occurs in:
quiz.why: Kaal baisakhi are violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms that hit West Bengal in the hot season. Mango showers are for Kerala and Karnataka.

quiz.q: Winter rain helps which crops?
quiz.why: Winter rain from western disturbances is good for rabi crops such as wheat, which are sown in winter and harvested in spring.

quiz.q: The Coromandel coast gets much rain in:
quiz.why: The Coromandel coast gets much of its rain in October–November from the retreating monsoon and cyclones in the Bay of Bengal.

lessons.title: Rainfall distribution and the monsoon as a unifying bond

scenes.text: In Punjab, Kerala and Assam, farmers time their sowing by the monsoon's arrival.
Festivals across India — from harvest celebrations to rain songs — revolve around the monsoon's rhythm.

steps.title: Distribution of rainfall
steps.body:
- **Over 400 cm**: western coast and north-east India.
- **Less than 60 cm**: western Rajasthan and adjoining parts of Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab; also the interior of the Deccan plateau and east of the Sahyadris; and Leh in Ladakh.
- Moderate rainfall elsewhere; **snowfall** in the Himalayas.
- Rainfall decreases from **east to west** in the northern plains and is highly **variable** — areas of low rainfall are prone to drought, areas of high rainfall to floods.

steps.title: Monsoon as a unifying bond
steps.body: The Himalayas protect India from extremely cold Central Asian winds, giving northern India uniformly higher temperatures than other areas at the same latitude. The peninsular plateau, with the sea on three sides, has moderate temperatures. Despite this moderation there are great variations, yet the **unity** of the Indian landscape, its people, animals and plants is shaped by the monsoon. The whole agricultural calendar, the life of the people, their festivities, all revolve around the monsoon. Year after year, people from north to south and east to west eagerly await its arrival. The rivers carry its water and the monsoon brings the entire subcontinent together.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why does rainfall decrease westwards in the northern plains? (3 marks)**
The Bay of Bengal branch moves up the Ganga plain from east to west; as it moves, moisture decreases, so Kolkata gets more rain than Patna, which gets more than Delhi; western Rajasthan gets the least.

**Q2. Why is the monsoon a unifying bond? (3 marks)**
It sets the agricultural calendar for the whole country; festivals and lifestyles depend on it; rivers it feeds flow across states; everyone awaits it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leh is a **low-rainfall** region (rain shadow/cold desert), not high.
- Rainfall decreases **east to west** in the north, but **west to east** across the Western Ghats in the south (rain shadow).

steps.title: Reading a climate graph
steps.body: On a climograph, bars show monthly rainfall and a line shows temperature. A tall bar in July and a falling temperature line from June means monsoon cloud cover is cooling the place.

bands.text: Low: western Rajasthan, Leh, interior Deccan — drought-prone
Moderate: much of the plains and plateau
High: eastern India, parts of the Western Ghats
Very high (400+ cm): western coast and north-east, e.g. Mawsynram

quiz.q: Which region gets over 400 cm of rain?
quiz.why: The western coast, the Western Ghats and the north-east get over 400 cm of rain, since they face the moisture-laden winds. Western Rajasthan and Leh are dry.

quiz.q: Rainfall in the northern plains decreases from:
quiz.why: Rainfall in the northern plains declines from east to west because the Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon loses moisture as it moves west.

quiz.q: Leh receives:
quiz.why: Leh in Ladakh gets less than 60 cm of rain a year, as it lies in a cold desert behind the Himalayas.

quiz.q: The monsoon is called a unifying bond because:
options: It blows only in the south
The agricultural calendar and festivals across India revolve around it
quiz.why: The monsoon is a unifying bond because the farming calendar, festivals and the whole life of the country revolve around its arrival. It does not bring snow or only blow in the south.

quiz.q: High rainfall variability makes low-rainfall areas prone to:
quiz.why: Where rainfall is low and varies a lot from year to year, the years of very little rain cause droughts. Floods are more likely where rainfall is high.

questions.q: The word 'monsoon' is derived from:
questions.why: The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season. It is not from Latin, Persian or Sanskrit.

questions.q: Loo is a:
questions.why: The loo is a strong, hot, dry wind that blows over the north and north-western plains in summer. It is not a current or cyclone.

questions.q: Mango showers occur in:
questions.why: Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka in summer, which help the ripening of mangoes.

questions.q: The cold weather season lasts from:
questions.why: The cold weather season in India lasts from mid-November to February, with falling temperatures in the north.

questions.q: Which wind brings winter rain to Tamil Nadu?
questions.why: The north-east trade winds, blowing from land to sea, pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and bring winter rain to Tamil Nadu. The south-west monsoon is the summer wind.

questions.q: The highest average rainfall in the world:
questions.why: Mawsynram in Meghalaya has the highest average rainfall in the world. Kochi, Mumbai and Darjeeling get heavy rain, but much less.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Coastal places like Mumbai have moderate climate. Reason (R): The sea moderates temperature.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The sea keeps temperatures moderate in coastal places like Mumbai, because water heats and cools slowly. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: In October a city has clear skies, high temperatures and high humidity after rains stop. This is:
questions.why: October heat is the hot, humid spell after the monsoon retreats: skies are clear and temperature and humidity rise. Loo and kaal baisakhi are summer events.

questions.q: Which is linked to a weaker Indian monsoon?
questions.why: El Niño, a warm current off Peru, is linked with weaker or failed Indian monsoons. La Niña often goes with stronger rain.

questions.q: Why does Chennai get little rain in July?
options: It lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats for the Arabian Sea branch and is parallel to the Bay branch
questions.why: In July Chennai lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats for the Arabian Sea branch, and parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch, so it gets little rain.

questions.q: If Mumbai gets 240 cm and Pune 70 cm a year, Pune gets about what percentage of Mumbai's rain?
questions.why: Percentage = 70 ÷ 240 × 100 ≈ 29%. Pune lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, so it gets much less than Mumbai.

questions.q: A place's temperature drops about 6.5°C per 1,000 m. If the plains are 30°C, a hill station at 2,000 m is about:
questions.why: Temperature falls 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, so at 2,000 m it falls 13 °C. 30 − 13 = 17 °C.

questions.q: Assertion (A): North India has higher temperatures than other areas at the same latitude. Reason (R): The Himalayas block cold Central Asian winds.
questions.why: Both are true. The Himalayas block cold winds from Central Asia, so north India stays warmer than other areas at the same latitude. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A farmer in Haryana sows wheat in November and is glad of light rain in January. Its source?
questions.why: Light January rain for the rabi wheat crop comes from western cyclonic disturbances, which bring winter rain to north India. Kaal baisakhi and mango showers occur in summer.

questions.q: Which combination best explains the 'burst' of the monsoon?
options: Sudden onset of moisture-laden winds with violent thunder and lightning when the low-pressure trough strengthens
questions.why: The 'burst' of the monsoon is its sudden arrival, with moisture-laden winds and violent thunder and lightning, when the low-pressure trough strengthens. It is not slow rain or dry winds.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Natural Vegetation and Wildlife
courses.summary: India's rich biodiversity, factors that shape vegetation, the five major vegetation types, wildlife and conservation efforts.
outcomes: Learners can explain factors affecting vegetation
Learners can describe the five vegetation types with rainfall and species
Learners can name important wildlife and their habitats
Learners can explain conservation measures such as biosphere reserves

lessons.title: Biodiversity and factors affecting vegetation

scenes.text: In the rainforests of Kerala, Neha can barely see the sky through tall evergreen trees.
In Kutch she sees thorny shrubs and cacti — the same country, very different plants.

steps.title: Biodiversity of India
steps.body:
India is one of the **12 mega biodiversity countries** of the world. With about **47,000 plant species**, India is 10th in the world and 4th in Asia in plant diversity. There are about **15,000 flowering plants** (about 6% of the world total), and many non-flowering plants such as ferns, algae and fungi. India also has about **90,000 species of animals** and a rich variety of fish.

**Natural vegetation** (virgin vegetation) is a plant community that has grown naturally without human aid. **Flora** = plants of an area; **fauna** = animals.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body:
- **Relief**: **land** (fertile plains used for crops; undulating terrain has grasslands and woodlands) and **soil** (sandy soils of the desert support cactus and thorny bushes; wet marshy deltaic soils support mangroves; hill slopes with deep soil have conical trees).
- **Climate**: **temperature** (vegetation changes with altitude in the Himalayas), **photoperiod** (sunlight — trees grow faster in summer), **precipitation** (heavy rain → dense vegetation).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Define natural vegetation. (1 mark)** Plants that grow naturally without human help and have been left undisturbed for long.

**Q2. How does rainfall affect vegetation? (2 marks)** Areas with heavy rainfall (200 cm+) have dense evergreen forests; areas with little rainfall have thorny scrub and grasses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cultivated crops and orchards are **not** natural vegetation.
- India's plant diversity rank: **10th in the world, 4th in Asia** — not 1st.

cards.back: Plants of a region or period
Animals of a region or period
Duration of sunlight affecting plant growth
One of 12 countries with extremely high biodiversity — India is one

quiz.q: India's rank in world plant diversity:
quiz.why: India ranks 10th in the world and 4th in Asia in plant diversity. The other ranks given are not correct.

quiz.q: Number of plant species in India is about:
quiz.why: India has about 47,000 plant species, which is a big share of the world's plant diversity.

quiz.q: Fauna means:
quiz.why: Fauna means the animals of a region, while flora means its plants. Rivers and soils are not fauna.

quiz.q: Which soil supports mangroves?
quiz.why: Mangroves grow in wet, marshy, salty deltaic soils in tidal areas. Black soil, desert sand and mountain soil do not suit them.

quiz.q: Is a mango orchard natural vegetation?
quiz.why: A mango orchard is planted and tended by humans, so it is not natural vegetation, which grows by itself without human help.

lessons.title: Tropical evergreen, deciduous and thorn forests

scenes.text: In a Madhya Pradesh forest, the teak trees shed their leaves in the dry summer.
A forest ranger explains: these are monsoon forests — they drop leaves to save water.

steps.title: Tropical evergreen forests
steps.body:
- Areas with **more than 200 cm** rainfall and a short dry season: **Western Ghats**, islands of Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar, upper parts of Assam and the Tamil Nadu coast.
- Trees reach great heights, up to 60 m; all kinds of vegetation — trees, shrubs, creepers — in a multilayered structure.
- No definite time for shedding leaves; appear **green all year**.
- Trees: **ebony, mahogany, rosewood, rubber, cinchona**.
- Animals: elephants, monkeys, lemurs, deer; one-horned rhinoceros in the jungles of Assam and West Bengal.

steps.title: Tropical deciduous forests
steps.body:
The most widespread forests of India, also called **monsoon forests**; rainfall **70–200 cm**. Trees shed leaves for about six to eight weeks in dry summer.
- **Moist deciduous** (100–200 cm): north-eastern states, foothills of the Himalayas, Jharkhand, West Odisha, Chhattisgarh, eastern slopes of the Western Ghats. **Teak** is the most dominant; also bamboo, sal, shisham, sandalwood, khair, kusum, arjun, mulberry.
- **Dry deciduous** (70–100 cm): rainier parts of the peninsular plateau and plains of Bihar and UP. Teak, sal, peepal, neem. Large areas cleared for cultivation.
- Animals: lion, tiger, pig, deer, elephant; many birds, lizards, snakes, tortoises.

steps.title: Tropical thorn forests and scrubs
steps.body: In regions with **less than 70 cm** rainfall: north-western India including semi-arid areas of Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, UP and Haryana. Trees: **acacias, palms, euphorbias, cacti**. Trees are scattered with long roots penetrating deep into the soil; stems succulent to conserve water; leaves mostly thick and small. Animals: rats, mice, rabbits, fox, wolf, tiger, lion, wild ass, horses, camels.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why are tropical evergreen forests 'evergreen'? (2 marks)** Trees shed leaves at different times, so the forest never looks bare — warm, wet climate all year.

**Q2. How are thorn-forest plants adapted to dryness? (3 marks)** Long deep roots; succulent stems storing water; small thick leaves (or thorns) to reduce evaporation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Teak** dominates **moist deciduous**, not evergreen forests.
- Thorn forests: **<70 cm**; dry deciduous: **70–100 cm**; moist deciduous: **100–200 cm**; evergreen: **>200 cm**.

activity.prompt: Which forest type?

quiz.q: Most widespread forests of India:
quiz.why: Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread forests in India. They shed leaves in the dry season.

quiz.q: Rainfall for tropical evergreen forests:
quiz.why: Tropical evergreen forests grow where annual rainfall is above 200 cm, and the heavy rain keeps the forest green all year.

quiz.q: Dominant tree of moist deciduous forests:
quiz.why: Teak is the most dominant tree of the moist deciduous forests. Mahogany grows in evergreen forests and Sundari in mangroves.

quiz.q: Cinchona grows in:
quiz.why: Cinchona is a tree of the tropical evergreen forests, which have heavy rainfall. It is not found in alpine meadows or thorn forests.

quiz.q: Thorn forest plants have:
quiz.why: Plants in thorn forests have long roots to reach water and succulent stems to store it, which suit dry conditions. Huge thin leaves would lose too much water.

lessons.title: Montane and mangrove forests

scenes.text: Trekking up a Himalayan slope, Kabir passes oak and chestnut, then pine and deodar.
Higher still he sees silver firs, birch, then alpine grasslands where Gujjars graze their herds.

steps.title: Montane forests
steps.body:
In mountains, temperature falls with altitude, so vegetation changes like it does from the tropics to the tundra.
- **1,000–2,000 m**: wet temperate forests — evergreen broad-leaved trees such as **oak and chestnut**.
- **1,500–3,000 m**: temperate forests with **coniferous** trees — **pine, deodar, silver fir, spruce, cedar** — on the southern slopes of the Himalayas and high-altitude parts of southern and north-east India.
- Higher: **temperate grasslands**.
- **Above 3,600 m**: **alpine vegetation** — silver fir, junipers, pines, birches; trees get stunted near the snow line. **Alpine grasslands** are used for grazing by nomadic tribes like the **Gujjars and Bakarwals**. At higher altitudes, mosses and lichens form part of **tundra** vegetation.
- Animals: Kashmir stag, spotted deer, wild sheep, jack rabbit, Tibetan antelope, yak, snow leopard, squirrels, shaggy-horn wild ibex, bear, red panda.

steps.title: Mangrove forests
steps.body:
Found in coastal areas influenced by **tides**; mud and silt accumulate. Dense mangroves are common; roots of plants are submerged under water.
- Found in deltas of the **Ganga, Mahanadi, Krishna, Godavari and Kaveri**.
- In the **Ganga-Brahmaputra delta**, **sundari** trees provide durable hard timber. Palm, coconut, keora and agar also grow.
- The **Royal Bengal Tiger** is the famous animal of these forests; also turtles, crocodiles, gharials and snakes.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why does vegetation change with altitude in the Himalayas? (2 marks)** Temperature drops with height, so plant types change from broad-leaved (lower) to coniferous to alpine.

**Q2. Name the delta where sundari trees are found, and one animal. (2 marks)** Ganga–Brahmaputra (Sundarban) delta; Royal Bengal Tiger.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mangroves grow in **tidal** coastal areas, not in mountains.
- Conifers grow at **1,500–3,000 m**; oak and chestnut lower (1,000–2,000 m).

activity.prompt: Order Himalayan vegetation from lowest to highest altitude
items: Wet temperate forest: oak and chestnut
Coniferous forest: pine and deodar
Temperate grasslands
Alpine vegetation: junipers and birches
Mosses and lichens (tundra)

quiz.q: Deodar is a:
quiz.why: The deodar is a coniferous tree found in the montane forests of the Himalayas. It is not a tropical, mangrove or thorn plant.

quiz.q: Alpine vegetation grows above:
quiz.why: Alpine vegetation grows above about 3,600 m, where it is very cold. Silver fir, junipers and birches grow there.

quiz.q: Sundari trees are found in:
quiz.why: Sundari trees grow in the Sundarbans, the mangrove area of the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta. The delta takes its name from them.

quiz.q: Which animal lives in montane forests?
quiz.why: The snow leopard lives in montane forests and high Himalayan areas. The wild ass lives in the Rann of Kachchh and the camel in the desert.

quiz.q: Mangroves grow where there are:
quiz.why: Mangroves grow along coasts where tides bring in salt water and mud. They are not found with lava, glaciers or dunes.

lessons.title: Wildlife and conservation

scenes.text: A century ago, Asiatic lions were reduced to a few in Gujarat's Gir forest.
Protection by the state and local communities helped their numbers grow again — proof that conservation works.

steps.title: Wildlife of India
steps.body:
- **Elephants**: hot wet forests of **Assam, Karnataka and Kerala**.
- **One-horned rhinoceros**: swampy and marshy lands of **Assam and West Bengal**.
- **Wild ass**: **Rann of Kachchh**; **camels** in the Thar desert.
- **Indian bison, nilgai, chousingha (four-horned antelope), gazel** and deer species.
- **Lion**: natural habitat is the **Gir forest in Gujarat** (Asiatic lion).
- **Tiger**: forests of MP, the Sundarbans of West Bengal and the Himalayan region.
- Ladakh: yak, shaggy-horned wild ox, Tibetan antelope, bharal (blue sheep), wild sheep, kiang (Tibetan wild ass), ibex, bear, snow leopard, red panda.
- Birds: **peacock** (national bird), pheasants, ducks, parakeets, cranes, pigeons.

steps.title: Threats and conservation
steps.body:
Threats: hunting for commercial purposes, pollution from chemicals and industrial waste, introduction of alien species, reckless cutting of forests for agriculture and habitation.

Steps taken:
- **Biosphere reserves**: **18** set up in India; many included in the UNESCO world network (e.g. Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar, Nilgiri).
- Financial and technical assistance to botanical gardens since 1992.
- **Project Tiger (1973)**, Project Rhino, Project Great Indian Bustard and others.
- National parks, wildlife sanctuaries and zoological gardens.
- **Wildlife Protection Act, 1972**.
- **Medicinal plants**: India has long used plants like **sarpagandha** (blood pressure), **jamun** (digestion; seeds for diabetes), **arjun** (heart), **babool** (leaves for eye sores), **neem** (antibiotic, antibacterial), **tulsi** (cough and cold), **kachnar** (asthma, ulcers).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why is the flora and fauna of India under threat? (3 marks)** Hunting/poaching for trade; pollution; alien species; deforestation for farming and settlement.

**Q2. What is a biosphere reserve? (2 marks)** A large protected area conserving the full ecosystem — plants, animals and people's traditional ways of life — for research and sustainable use. India has 18.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Lions live in **Gir (Gujarat)**, not the Sundarbans (which have tigers).
- One-horned rhino: **Assam and West Bengal**, not Rajasthan.
- Project Tiger began in **1973**; the Wildlife Protection Act was **1972**.

activity.prompt: Match the animal with its habitat

quiz.q: How many biosphere reserves in India (as per the chapter)?
quiz.why: India has 18 biosphere reserves, as per the chapter. Biosphere reserves protect whole ecosystems.

quiz.q: Project Tiger began in:
quiz.why: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to protect tigers. The Wildlife Protection Act was passed in 1972, which is a different year.

quiz.q: Which medicinal plant is used for blood pressure?
quiz.why: Sarpagandha is the medicinal plant used for treating high blood pressure. Tulsi is used for colds, and babool and kachnar have other uses.

quiz.q: The wild ass is found in:
quiz.why: The wild ass is found in the Rann of Kachchh in Gujarat. Gir has lions, Kaziranga rhinos and the Sundarbans tigers.

quiz.q: The Wildlife Protection Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The Wildlife (Protection) Act was passed in 1972 to protect wild animals and their habitats.

questions.q: India's national bird:
questions.why: The peacock is India's national bird. Cranes, parakeets and pigeons are other birds.

questions.q: Teak is a tree of:
questions.why: Teak is a tree of tropical deciduous forests, particularly moist deciduous ones. It is not found in alpine, thorn or mangrove forests.

questions.q: Asiatic lions live in:
questions.why: Asiatic lions live in the Gir forest of Gujarat. The Sundarbans, Corbett and Kaziranga are known for tigers or rhinos.

questions.q: India is one of how many mega biodiversity countries?
questions.why: India is one of the 12 mega biodiversity countries of the world. 18 is the number of biosphere reserves.

questions.q: Mangrove forests grow in:
questions.why: Mangrove forests grow in tidal deltas and coastal areas where salty and fresh water meet. They do not grow in mountains or deserts.

questions.q: Which is a thorn forest plant?
questions.why: Euphorbia is a thorny, succulent plant of dry thorn forests. Rosewood, Sundari and Deodar belong to other forest types.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Tropical evergreen forests look green all year. Reason (R): Trees shed leaves at different times.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Trees in evergreen forests shed leaves at different times, so no season is bare, and the forest looks green all year. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A forest with rainfall of 85 cm has teak, sal and neem, much of it cleared for farms. Type?
questions.why: Rainfall of 70–100 cm with teak, sal and neem indicates dry deciduous forests. Moist deciduous forests get 100–200 cm, and thorn forests less than 70 cm.

questions.q: Which is wrongly matched?
questions.why: Arjun is used for heart trouble, not eye sores. The other pairs are correct: jamun for digestion, tulsi for cough and cold, and neem as an antibiotic.

questions.q: Coniferous forests in the Himalayas grow between:
questions.why: Coniferous forests in the Himalayas grow between about 1,500 and 3,000 m. Above 3,600 m is alpine vegetation.

questions.q: If India has 47,000 plant species and 15,000 flowering plants, what percentage of its plant species are flowering?
questions.why: Share = 15,000 ÷ 47,000 × 100 ≈ 31.9%, or about 32%. Divide the part by the whole.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Thorn forest trees have long roots. Reason (R): They must reach underground water in dry areas.
questions.why: Both are true. Thorn forest trees have long roots because water lies deep underground in dry regions. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Why are biosphere reserves better for conservation than zoos alone?
options: They protect whole ecosystems, including local people's sustainable use
questions.why: Biosphere reserves protect whole ecosystems, with their plants, animals and the sustainable use by local people. Zoos keep animals in cages and protect only individual species.

questions.q: Case: A trekker sees stunted junipers and birches, then mosses and lichens near snow. Altitude?
questions.why: Stunted junipers and birches, with mosses and lichens near snow, show alpine and tundra vegetation, found above about 3,600 m.

questions.q: Which human activity most directly threatens the one-horned rhinoceros?
options: Poaching for horn and loss of swampy habitat
questions.why: The one-horned rhinoceros is endangered by poaching for its horn and by the loss of its swampy habitat. Snowfall and coral bleaching are not direct threats.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Population
courses.summary: India's population size and distribution, density, growth and its processes, and population characteristics such as age, sex ratio and literacy — with calculations.
outcomes: Learners can describe the size and distribution of India's population
Learners can calculate density, growth and growth rate
Learners can explain birth rate, death rate and migration
Learners can interpret age composition, sex ratio and literacy, and explain the National Population Policy

lessons.title: Size, distribution and density

scenes.text: An enumerator knocks at Rahul's home and asks how many people live there, their ages and education.
Millions of such visits together become the Census — India's count of its people every ten years.

steps.title: The census
steps.body:
The **census** is the official enumeration of population done periodically. In India the first census was held in **1872**; the first complete census was taken in **1881**. Since then, a census has been held every **ten years**.

According to **Census 2011**, India's population was **1,210.6 million** (about 121 crore) — about **17.5%** of the world's population, living on only 2.4% of the world's area.

steps.title: Distribution and density
steps.body:
- **Uttar Pradesh** is the most populous state (about **199 million**, about 16% of India). **Sikkim** has about 0.6 million; Lakshadweep only about 64,000.
- Almost half of India's population lives in just five states: UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh (undivided).
- **Population density** = number of persons per unit area. India's density in 2011: **382 persons per sq km**. Highest: **Bihar (1,102)**; lowest: **Arunachal Pradesh (17)**.
- Low density (<250): hilly, dissected, rugged areas with unfavourable climate (Assam, most peninsular states have moderate). High density: northern plains and Kerala (fertile soil, plentiful rain).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Density of a district with 9,00,000 people in 1,500 sq km.**
Density = 9,00,000 ÷ 1,500 = **600 persons per sq km**.

**Ex 2. Check India's density.**
1,210.6 million ÷ 3.287 million sq km ≈ **368**. (The census figure of 382 uses a slightly different area base that excludes certain disputed areas, so the result is close.)

**Ex 3. Why is Bihar densely populated but Arunachal not?** Bihar: fertile flat plains, farming; Arunachal: rugged hills, forests, harsh terrain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Density is **persons per sq km**, not total population.
- Most populous ≠ most densely populated: UP is most populous; Bihar is most dense.
- The census is every **10** years, not 5.

activity.prompt: A town has 48,000 people living on 12 sq km. What is its population density?

quiz.q: India's population in 2011 was about:
quiz.why: India's 2011 census population was about 1,210.6 million, which is about 121 crore.

quiz.q: India's share of the world population (2011):
quiz.why: India has about 17.5% of the world's population, even though it has only 2.4% of its land area.

quiz.q: The most populous state is:
quiz.why: Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state, with about 200 million people in 2011. Maharashtra is second.

quiz.q: Highest density state (2011):
quiz.why: Bihar had the highest density among the states in 2011, about 1,102 persons per sq km. Kerala and West Bengal were also dense, but less than Bihar.

quiz.q: The first complete census was in:
quiz.why: The first complete census of India was held in 1881. An earlier attempt in 1872 was not complete.

lessons.title: Population growth and its processes

scenes.text: Grandma remembers that in her childhood many babies died young and families were large.
Now there's a health centre; fewer babies die, families are smaller, and some young people migrate to cities.

steps.title: Growth and growth rate
steps.body:
**Population growth** = change in the number of inhabitants during a specific period, expressed as **absolute numbers** (later population − earlier population) or as a **percentage change per year** (growth rate).

India's population grew steadily from 1951 (about 361 million) to 2011 (1,210.6 million). The **annual growth rate** has been declining since 1981. Even a declining rate on a large base means a big **absolute increase** each year.

steps.title: Three processes of change
steps.body:
1. **Birth rate**: number of live births per thousand persons in a year — a major component of growth; in India birth rates have always been higher than death rates.
2. **Death rate**: number of deaths per thousand persons in a year. A rapid fall in death rate (after 1951, better health facilities) was the main cause of rapid growth.
3. **Migration**: movement of people across regions. **Internal** migration (within the country) does not change total population but changes distribution; **international** migration changes the total. In India most internal migration is **rural to urban** — 'push' factors (poverty, unemployment in villages) and 'pull' factors (jobs and better living in cities).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Absolute increase 2001–2011.** 2001: 1,028.7 million; 2011: 1,210.6 million. Increase = **181.9 million**.

**Ex 2. Decadal growth rate.** 181.9 ÷ 1,028.7 × 100 ≈ **17.7%** per decade (about 1.64% a year).

**Ex 3. Natural growth.** A town has birth rate 22 and death rate 7 per thousand. Natural growth rate = 22 − 7 = **15 per thousand = 1.5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A falling growth **rate** does not mean the population is shrinking — it still increases.
- Internal migration does **not** change national population size.
- Rates are **per thousand**, not per hundred.

activity.prompt: Birth rate = 20 per 1000, death rate = 8 per 1000. What is the natural growth rate in percent?

quiz.q: The main cause of rapid population growth in India after 1951:
quiz.why: After 1951 the death rate fell rapidly because of better health care and food, while the birth rate stayed high. This caused rapid growth.

quiz.q: Birth rate is expressed per:
quiz.why: Birth rate is the number of live births per thousand people in a year. It is not per hundred or per family.

quiz.q: Which migration changes the distribution but not the total?
quiz.why: Internal migration moves people within the country, which changes the distribution but not the total. International migration changes the total of countries.

quiz.q: Most internal migration in India is:
quiz.why: Most internal migration in India is from rural to urban areas, as people seek jobs and better facilities in cities.

quiz.q: Absolute increase from 1,028.7 million to 1,210.6 million is:
quiz.why: Increase = 1,210.6 − 1,028.7 = 181.9 million. Subtract the old figure from the new one.

lessons.title: Age composition, sex ratio and literacy

scenes.text: Class 9 students survey their village: how many children, working adults and elderly?
They find more boys than girls in the under-6 group and ask their teacher why.

steps.title: Age composition
steps.body:
Number of people in different age groups:
- **Children (below 15)**: economically unproductive; need food, clothing, education and medical care.
- **Working age (15–59)**: economically productive and biologically reproductive.
- **Aged (above 59)**: may be economically productive (some retire); may work voluntarily.
A higher share of children and aged means a higher **dependency** on the working group.

steps.title: Sex ratio and literacy
steps.body:
- **Sex ratio** = number of **females per 1,000 males**. Census 2011: about **943** (provisional figures showed 940). **Kerala** has the highest (about 1,084); some states and UTs have very low ratios. The low ratio reflects historical discrimination against girls.
- **Literacy**: a person aged **7 years and above** who can read and write with understanding in any language is literate. Literacy rate in 2011: **about 74%** — males about 82%, females about 65%.
- **Occupational structure**: primary (agriculture, fishing, mining), secondary (manufacturing, construction), tertiary (transport, communication, commerce, administration). In India about 64% of people work in primary activities (older figure from the textbook period); the share in secondary and tertiary has been rising.
- **Health**: death rate fell from 25 per 1,000 in 1951 to 7.2 in 2011; life expectancy rose from 36.7 years in 1951 to about 67.9 years in 2011.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. A village has 2,400 males and 2,160 females. Sex ratio?**
2,160 ÷ 2,400 × 1,000 = **900 females per 1,000 males**.

**Ex 2. Literacy rate.** Of 5,000 people aged 7+, 3,900 are literate. Rate = 3,900 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = **78%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sex ratio is **females per 1,000 males**, not males per 1,000 females.
- Literacy counts people **aged 7+**; children under 7 are excluded.
- Working age group is **15–59**, not 18–60.

activity.prompt: A town has 5,000 males and 4,750 females. Calculate the sex ratio (females per 1,000 males).

quiz.q: Sex ratio means:
quiz.why: Sex ratio is the number of females per 1,000 males. It does not mean males per 1,000 females.

quiz.q: Which state has the highest sex ratio?
quiz.why: Kerala has the highest sex ratio in India. Haryana and Punjab have low ratios.

quiz.q: A literate person must be at least:
quiz.why: In the census, a person aged 7 or above who can read and write with understanding is counted as literate.

quiz.q: India's literacy rate in 2011 was about:
quiz.why: India's literacy rate was about 74% in 2011. The other values are not correct for that year.

quiz.q: The working age group is:
quiz.why: The working-age group is 15–59 years. Those aged 0–14 are children, and 60 or more are elderly.

lessons.title: Adolescents and the National Population Policy

scenes.text: One in five Indians is an adolescent, aged 10 to 19 — like Simran and her classmates.
Their school nurse explains why good nutrition, education and health care in these years shape India's future.

steps.title: Adolescent population
steps.body: **Adolescents** are generally grouped in the age group **10 to 19 years**. They form about one-fifth of India's population and are the country's most important resource for the future. Their nutritional requirements are higher than those of a normal child or adult; poor nutrition can lead to deficiency and stunted growth. Many adolescent girls suffer from **anaemia**. Awareness through literacy and education, and health programmes, can improve their wellbeing.

steps.title: National Population Policy (NPP) 2000
steps.body:
Recognising planned families, India started a comprehensive **Family Planning Programme in 1952**. The **NPP 2000** provides a policy framework:
- Free and compulsory school education up to 14 years of age
- Reducing the **infant mortality rate** to below 30 per 1,000 live births
- Universal immunisation of children against all vaccine-preventable diseases
- Promoting delayed marriage for girls
- Making family welfare a people-centred programme
**NPP 2000 and adolescents**: protecting them from unwanted pregnancies and sexually transmitted diseases; encouraging delayed marriage and child-bearing; education about risks of unprotected sex; making contraceptive services accessible; food supplements and nutrition services; strengthening legal measures to prevent child marriage.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why are adolescents important for India? (2 marks)** They form about a fifth of the population and will be the future workforce, parents and leaders; their health and education decide India's future.

**Q2. State three objectives of NPP 2000. (3 marks)** Free compulsory schooling up to 14; IMR below 30 per 1,000; universal immunisation; delayed marriage for girls.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Family planning began in **1952**; NPP in **2000** — don't mix the years.
- Adolescents = **10–19**, not 13–19.

steps.title: Healthy adolescence
steps.body: Iron-rich foods (green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery), regular check-ups and staying in school are simple steps. School health programmes provide iron-folic acid supplements to fight anaemia.

activity.prompt: Which NPP 2000 aims can your school or family support?
items: Every child up to 14 attends school
All children receive vaccines on schedule
Girls are not married before the legal age
Adolescents get iron-rich nutritious food
Correct health information is available to teenagers

quiz.q: Adolescents are aged:
quiz.why: Adolescents are people aged 10 to 19 years. They are about one-fifth of India's population.

quiz.q: India's Family Planning Programme began in:
quiz.why: India's Family Planning Programme was launched in 1952, early after Independence. It was one of the first in the world.

quiz.q: NPP 2000 aims to reduce IMR to below:
quiz.why: The National Population Policy 2000 aims to bring the infant mortality rate below 30 per 1,000 live births.

quiz.q: A common health problem of adolescent girls in India is:
quiz.why: Anaemia, caused by iron deficiency, is a common health problem among adolescent girls in India. Malaria, diabetes and polio are less closely linked.

quiz.q: NPP 2000 promotes free compulsory education up to age:
quiz.why: The National Population Policy 2000 promotes free and compulsory school education up to age 14.

questions.q: The census in India is held every:
questions.why: The census in India is held every 10 years. The first complete census was in 1881.

questions.q: Lowest density state in 2011:
questions.why: Arunachal Pradesh had the lowest density in 2011, about 17 persons per sq km, because of rugged hills and forests.

questions.q: The working age group is:
questions.why: The working-age group is 15–59 years. 10–19 is the adolescent group.

questions.q: India's population density in 2011:
questions.why: India's population density in 2011 was 382 persons per sq km. 1,102 is Bihar's density.

questions.q: Migration that changes total national population:
questions.why: International migration changes the total population of a country, as people leave or enter. Moves within a district or state only change the distribution.

questions.q: NPP was announced in:
questions.why: The National Population Policy was announced in the year 2000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): India's population kept rising after 1981 though the growth rate declined. Reason (R): A smaller rate on a very large base still adds large absolute numbers.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The growth rate fell after 1981, but a smaller rate on a very large base still adds many people. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: Young men leave a drought-hit village for factory jobs in Surat. 'Drought' is a ___ factor and 'jobs' a ___ factor.
questions.why: Drought pushes people out of the village, so it is a push factor; jobs in Surat attract them, so they are a pull factor. Push factors are at the origin and pull factors at the destination.

questions.q: Which is NOT an objective of NPP 2000?
questions.why: NPP 2000 aims at universal immunisation, lowering IMR below 30 and free schooling up to 14, and it discourages child marriage; it does not encourage it.

questions.q: Why is Kerala's sex ratio high compared to many states?
options: High literacy, better health care and women's status
questions.why: Kerala's high sex ratio comes from high literacy, better health care and the better status of women. Low literacy or female mortality would lower it.

questions.q: A district has 3,20,000 males and 3,04,000 females. Sex ratio?
questions.why: Sex ratio = females ÷ males × 1,000 = 304,000 ÷ 320,000 × 1,000 = 950 females per 1,000 males.

questions.q: Population grows from 50,000 to 56,000 in a decade. Decadal growth rate?
Birth rate 25, death rate 10, net out-migration 5 per 1,000. Overall growth rate?
questions.why: Natural increase = 25 − 10 = 15 per 1,000, and net out-migration removes 5, so 15 − 5 = 10 per 1,000, which is 1%. Divide by 10 to convert per 1,000 to per cent.

questions.q: Case: A state has rugged hills, dense forests and poor transport. Predict its density compared to the national average.
questions.why: Rugged hills, dense forests and poor transport make settlement difficult, so density would be much lower than average, as in Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.q: If 20% of 121 crore people are adolescents, how many adolescents is that?
questions.why: 20% of 121 crore = 0.2 × 121 = 24.2 crore. To find 20%, multiply by 0.2.

school-c9-social-c.title: Class 9 Social Science · Political Science (Democratic Politics – I)
school-c9-social-c.description: Chapter-by-chapter Class 9 Political Science: what democracy is and why, constitutional design, electoral politics, working of institutions and democratic rights — with real cases, solved answers and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · What is Democracy? Why Democracy?
courses.summary: A working definition of democracy, its four key features tested against real countries, arguments for and against, and the broader meaning of democracy.
outcomes: Learners can define democracy and state its key features
Learners can test real cases (Pakistan, China, Mexico, Zimbabwe, Saudi Arabia) against those features
Learners can weigh arguments for and against democracy
Learners can explain why democracy is a better form of government

lessons.title: A simple definition and the first two features

scenes.text: Class 9B is choosing a monitor. Last year the teacher simply appointed one; this year students will vote.
But the teacher still decides everything important. Is this really a democracy? The class debates.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
**Democracy is a form of government in which the rulers are elected by the people.** This simple definition separates democracies from monarchies, military dictatorships and one-party rule. But it needs to be refined into features:
1. Major decisions by **elected leaders**
2. **Free and fair electoral competition**
3. **One person, one vote, one value**
4. **Rule of law and respect for rights**

steps.title: Feature 1: Elected leaders take final decisions
steps.body:
**Pakistan**: In **October 1999** General **Pervez Musharraf** led a military coup, overthrew an elected government and declared himself 'Chief Executive'; in 2002 a referendum extended his term. Elections were held to national and provincial assemblies, but the final power rested with military officers and him; he could dismiss assemblies.

Lesson: elections alone are not enough — **final decision-making power must rest with those elected by the people.**

steps.title: Feature 2: Free and fair electoral competition
steps.body:
**China**: elections are held regularly (every five years) for the National People's Congress, but candidates need the approval of the **Chinese Communist Party**; the government is always formed by the Communist Party.

**Mexico**: since independence in 1930 it held elections every six years, but until **2000** every election was won by the **PRI (Institutional Revolutionary Party)**, using dirty tricks — government employees forced to attend party meetings, media ignoring opposition, polling booths shifted at the last minute.

Lesson: elections must offer a **real choice** — people must be able to remove current rulers.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why is Pakistan under Musharraf not a democracy? (3 marks)**
- He came to power through a military coup, not election.
- Elected assemblies existed, but final powers lay with him and the military.
- Rulers were not accountable to the people.

**Q2. Why were Mexico's elections not free and fair? (2 marks)** One party (PRI) won every election till 2000 by unfair practices; opposition had no real chance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Holding elections does **not** automatically make a country democratic (China, Mexico before 2000).
- PRI ruled Mexico until **2000**, not 2010.
- Musharraf's coup was in **1999**.

activity.prompt: Which feature of democracy is missing?

items.text: China — candidates need Communist Party approval
Mexico before 2000 — PRI always won by unfair tricks
An army general can dismiss elected assemblies

quiz.q: Democracy is a form of government in which rulers are:
quiz.why: In a democracy the rulers are elected by the people. Rulers who are appointed by a king, hereditary or chosen by the army are not democratic.

quiz.q: Musharraf came to power in Pakistan in:
quiz.why: General Pervez Musharraf took power in Pakistan through a military coup in October 1999. Elections were later held under his rule.

quiz.q: Until 2000, Mexico's elections were always won by:
quiz.why: Until 2000, Mexico's presidential elections were always won by the PRI (Institutional Revolutionary Party), as it used fraud and pressure to stay in power.

quiz.q: In China, the government is always formed by:
quiz.why: In China, elections are held but only candidates approved by the Chinese Communist Party can win, so the government is always formed by it.

quiz.q: Free and fair competition means:
options: People have a real choice to remove current rulers
quiz.why: Free and fair competition means people have a real choice and can remove the current rulers. One-party contests or army supervision do not allow this.

lessons.title: One person one vote, and rule of law

story.title: A vote that counts the same

scenes.text: In 2015 Saudi women vote for the first time in local elections.
Meanwhile, in another country, people who criticise the ruler are harassed by police. Two different failures of democracy.

steps.title: Feature 3: One person, one vote, one value
steps.body:
Democracy rests on **political equality**: each adult citizen must have one vote and each vote must have equal value.
- Until **2015**, women in **Saudi Arabia** did not have the right to vote.
- **Estonia** made its citizenship rules such that people belonging to the **Russian minority** find it difficult to get the right to vote.
- In **Fiji**, the electoral system was such that the vote of an indigenous Fijian had more value than that of an Indian-Fijian.

steps.title: Feature 4: Rule of law and respect for rights
steps.body:
**Zimbabwe** attained independence from white minority rule in **1980**. It was ruled by **ZANU-PF**, led by **Robert Mugabe**, who won elections regularly but by unfair practices; he changed the constitution several times to increase the President's powers; opposition workers were harassed; public protests and demonstrations against the government were declared illegal; there was a law limiting the right to criticise the President; television and radio were controlled; courts' judgments against the government were disregarded and judges pressured. He ruled until **2017**.

Lesson: a democratic government rules within limits set by constitutional law and citizens' rights; popular governments can be undemocratic.

steps.title: Summary definition
Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why is Zimbabwe under Mugabe not considered democratic? (3 marks)** Unfair elections; constitution changed to boost President's power; opposition harassed; protests banned; media controlled; court judgments ignored.

**Q2. Give two examples where 'one person one vote one value' was denied. (2 marks)** Saudi women before 2015; Russian minority in Estonia; unequal vote value in Fiji.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Popular' is not the same as 'democratic' — Mugabe was popular yet undemocratic.
- Saudi women got the vote in **2015** (local elections).

activity.prompt: Match the country to the democratic failure
pairs: Russian minority finds it hard to vote
No respect for rule of law and rights
Final power with an unelected ruler

quiz.q: Saudi women got the right to vote in:
quiz.why: Women in Saudi Arabia got the right to vote in 2015, much later than in most countries.

quiz.q: Zimbabwe became independent in:
quiz.why: Zimbabwe became independent from White minority rule in 1980. Mugabe's party then dominated its politics.

quiz.q: Mugabe's party was:
quiz.why: Robert Mugabe led ZANU-PF, which ruled Zimbabwe after independence. ANC is South Africa's party and PRI is Mexico's.

quiz.q: In Fiji, the problem was:
quiz.why: In Fiji, the votes of indigenous Fijians had more value than the votes of Indo-Fijians. So the problem was the unequal value of votes.

quiz.q: A democratic government must work within:
quiz.why: A democratic government must act within constitutional law and respect citizens' rights. It cannot just follow its ruler's, army's or party's wishes.

lessons.title: Arguments against and for democracy

story.title: A debate in the staff room

scenes.text: Mr Verma says: 'Democracy is slow. Leaders keep changing. A strong ruler would fix everything fast.'
Ms Iyer replies: 'Fast, yes — but who corrects a strong ruler's mistakes? In democracy, we can.'

steps.title: Arguments against democracy
steps.body:
- Leaders keep changing, leading to **instability**.
- Democracy is about political **competition and power play**; no scope for morality.
- So many people have to be consulted that it leads to **delays**.
- Elected leaders **do not know the best interest** of the people; it leads to bad decisions.
- Leads to **corruption** because it is based on electoral competition.
- **Ordinary people** don't know what is good for them; they should not decide anything.

steps.title: Arguments for democracy
steps.body:
1. **More accountable** form of government — responds to people's needs. Example: China's famine of **1958–1961** was one of the worst recorded famines, killing nearly **three crore** people; India's economic condition was not much better, yet it did not have a famine of that kind. Economists believe this was due to different government policies — the existence of democracy made the Indian government respond to food scarcity.
2. **Improves the quality of decision-making** — based on consultation and discussion.
3. Provides a method to **deal with differences and conflicts**.
4. **Enhances the dignity** of citizens — based on political equality.
5. Allows us to **correct its own mistakes** — public discussion and the possibility of changing rulers.

Democracy is **better** than other forms of government, though it cannot guarantee everything.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Give the famine example in favour of democracy. (3 marks)** China's 1958–61 famine killed nearly 3 crore people; India, poor too, had no such famine because a democratic government had to respond to food scarcity and could be criticised by the press and opposition.

**Q2. 'Democracy leads to delays.' Answer this objection. (2 marks)** Consultation takes time, but it improves the quality of decisions and reduces costly mistakes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Don't claim democracy removes all corruption or poverty — the chapter says it is better, not perfect.
- The famine example is **China 1958–61**, not India.

activity.prompt: For or against democracy?

items.text: It allows us to correct mistakes
It enhances the dignity of citizens
It is more accountable to people's needs

quiz.q: China's great famine occurred in:
quiz.why: China's great famine was in 1958–61, during which about three crore people died. The Cultural Revolution was 1966–76.

quiz.q: About how many people died in that famine?
quiz.why: Nearly three crore (30 million) people died in China's famine of 1958–61. 3 lakh would be far too few.

quiz.q: Which is an argument FOR democracy?
quiz.why: An argument for democracy is that it improves the quality of decision-making, since decisions follow consultation. Delay, instability and corruption are criticisms.

quiz.q: Democracy enhances dignity because it is based on:
quiz.why: Democracy enhances dignity because it is based on political equality, with every adult having one equal vote. Wealth, religion or force do not.

quiz.q: Democracy is better because it:
quiz.why: Democracy is better because mistakes can be corrected, as people can change leaders and policies. It is not perfect and does not avoid discussion.

lessons.title: The broader meanings of democracy

scenes.text: The Sharma family must decide whether to move cities. Grandfather, parents and children each give views.
They decide together. Their teacher says: 'That is democracy too — in a family.'

steps.title: Representative democracy
steps.body: The most common form today is **representative democracy**: the majority rules through elected representatives. Why? Modern democracies involve millions of people, so they cannot sit together and make collective decisions; even if they could, citizens don't have the time, desire or skills to take part in all decisions.

steps.title: Democracy beyond government
steps.body:
The word democracy is also used for organisations other than government — a family, a class, a club. A democratic decision involves consultation with and consent of all who are affected. Democracy is also a **principle** for all spheres of life.

A democratic government is better than a non-democratic one, but we can make it **better**: there is no perfect democracy anywhere; every country can improve. Citizens' participation — not only voting but also discussing, protesting peacefully and asking questions — makes democracy deeper.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why do modern democracies use representatives? (2 marks)** Millions of people cannot meet together; citizens lack time, desire or skills to take all decisions.

**Q2. 'Democracy is not just a form of government.' Explain. (3 marks)** It can apply to families, schools and organisations; it is a principle of consultation and consent; it requires active citizens beyond elections.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Representative democracy is not 'less democratic' — it is a practical necessity.
- Democracy is a **process**; no country is a 'perfect' democracy.

activity.prompt: Think of a decision in your family, class or club. Was it taken democratically? What would make it more democratic?
activity.hint: Who was consulted? Did everyone affected have a voice? Could the decision be reviewed later?

quiz.q: The most common form of democracy today is:
quiz.why: Representative democracy, where people elect their representatives to decide for them, is the most common form today. Direct democracy is practical only for small groups.

quiz.q: Why can't all citizens take every decision directly?
options: They are too many and lack time/skills
quiz.why: Citizens cannot decide everything directly because there are too many of them and they lack the time and skills. It is not because of any ban.

quiz.q: Democracy can apply to:
quiz.why: Democracy is a general principle that can apply to families, schools and other organisations as well as governments.

quiz.q: Is there a perfect democracy anywhere?
quiz.why: No democracy is perfect, and every democracy can improve. Citizens must keep working to deepen it.

quiz.q: A democratic decision involves:
options: Consultation with and consent of those affected
quiz.why: A democratic decision involves consultation with and the consent of those affected. Orders from the top or secret meetings are not democratic.

questions.q: Democracy is a form of government in which rulers are:
questions.why: Democracy is government by rulers elected by the people. Hereditary, priestly or army rule are not democratic.

questions.q: Who led the 1999 coup in Pakistan?
questions.why: General Pervez Musharraf led the 1999 coup in Pakistan against Nawaz Sharif. Zia-ul-Haq and Ayub Khan were earlier military rulers.

questions.q: Robert Mugabe ruled:
questions.why: Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for decades, with ZANU-PF dominating elections. He was not a leader of South Africa, Kenya or Nigeria.

questions.q: The PRI ruled which country until 2000?
questions.why: The PRI ruled Mexico for over seventy years until 2000. Spain, Chile and Brazil did not have this party rule.

questions.q: Which feature is violated when one group's votes count more?
options: One person, one vote, one value
questions.why: One person, one vote, one value means all votes should count equally. If one group's votes count more, as in Fiji, this principle is violated.

questions.q: Which is an argument against democracy?
questions.why: An argument against democracy is that frequent changes of leaders cause instability. Dignity, correction of mistakes and accountability are arguments for it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Regular elections in China do not make it a democracy. Reason (R): Candidates need approval of the Communist Party, so there is no real choice.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. In China all candidates need the Communist Party's approval, so people lack a real choice, and regular elections alone do not make it a democracy. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A President bans protests, controls TV, ignores court rulings but wins elections regularly. Which feature is missing most clearly?
options: Rule of law and respect for rights
questions.why: Banning protests, controlling TV and ignoring courts show a lack of rule of law and respect for rights, as in Zimbabwe. Elections alone do not make a democracy.

questions.q: What does the China–India famine comparison show?
options: Democratic governments are more responsive to people's needs
questions.why: India's democracy avoided a famine like China's, which shows democratic governments are more responsive to people's needs because they face voters. It does not mean democracies never have shortages.

questions.q: Why is representative democracy necessary?
options: Large populations cannot directly make all decisions
questions.why: Large populations cannot all take every decision directly because of scale and time, so people elect representatives. It is not about kings or cost.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A popular leader is always democratic. Reason (R): Mugabe won elections.
questions.why: The assertion is false because popularity does not make a leader democratic. The reason is true, since Mugabe won elections, but he still ruled undemocratically. So only R is true.

questions.q: In a country, 60 lakh voters elect 60 members while another region's 20 lakh voters elect 40 members. What principle is broken?
questions.why: The first region needs 1 lakh voters per seat and the second only 50,000, so a vote in the second counts twice as much. This breaks the principle of equal value of votes.

questions.q: Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Democracy is better than other forms because it is accountable and allows correction
questions.why: Democracy is better because it is accountable and allows corrections, but it does not guarantee prosperity or avoid conflict. The other statements are false or too narrow.

questions.q: Case: A state holds elections but the army chief can dismiss the assembly any time. A student says it is democratic because elections happen. Best rebuttal?
options: Final decision-making power must lie with elected representatives
questions.why: Elections mean little if the army chief can dismiss the assembly. In a democracy, the final decision-making power must lie with elected representatives, as the Musharraf example showed.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the four features of democracy?
options: Elected leaders decide; free and fair competition; one person one vote one value; rule of law and rights
questions.why: The four features are elected leaders take the decisions, free and fair electoral competition, one person one vote one value, and rule of law and rights. The other sets are mixed-up.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Constitutional Design
courses.summary: Why democracies need constitutions, South Africa's journey from apartheid to democracy, how India's Constitution was made, and the values in its Preamble.
outcomes: Learners can explain why a constitution is needed
