Learners can describe non-farm activities and their importance

lessons.title: Palampur and the organisation of production

story.title: A village with a bus stop

scenes.text: Palampur, an imaginary village, is linked by an all-weather road to Raiganj, 3 km away. Buses, bullock carts, tongas and motorcycles use it.
Most homes have electricity, which runs tubewells in fields. There are schools and a health centre.

steps.title: About Palampur
steps.body: Palampur is a **hypothetical village** used to understand production. **Farming** is the main activity; other activities include small-scale manufacturing, dairy and transport. Palampur has about **450 families** belonging to several castes. About 150 families of the dalits (SCs) live in one corner; they are mostly landless or own small plots. It has well-developed roads, electricity, two primary schools, one high school, a primary health centre and a private dispensary.

steps.title: Four factors of production
steps.body:
The aim of production is to produce goods and services we want. Four requirements:
1. **Land** and other natural resources such as water, forests, minerals.
2. **Labour** — people who do the work; some need to be highly educated, others do manual work.
3. **Physical capital** — inputs required at every stage:
   - **Fixed capital**: tools, machines, buildings — used over many years (e.g. tubewells, tractors, generators).
   - **Working capital**: raw materials and money in hand — used up in production (e.g. seeds, fertilisers, cash to pay wages).
4. **Human capital** — knowledge and enterprise to put together land, labour and physical capital and produce output (the entrepreneur).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Classify as fixed or working capital: tractor, seeds, tubewell, money for wages. (2 marks)**
Fixed: tractor, tubewell. Working: seeds, money for wages.

**Q2. Why is human capital necessary? (2 marks)** Someone must have the knowledge and enterprise to combine the other factors and decide what and how to produce.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Money in hand is **working** capital, not fixed.
- Palampur is **hypothetical** — not a real village to locate on a map.
- Human capital ≠ labour: it means knowledge and enterprise.

activity.prompt: Classify each item

quiz.q: The main production activity in Palampur:
quiz.why: Farming is the main production activity in Palampur, and most people depend on it for their living. Other activities like dairy are small.

quiz.q: Which is fixed capital?
quiz.why: A tubewell is fixed capital because it is used in production for many years. Raw materials, cash and seeds get used up in production.

quiz.q: Working capital includes:
options: Raw materials and money in hand
quiz.why: Working capital includes raw materials and money in hand, which are used up in production. Land, buildings and machines are fixed capital.

quiz.q: Knowledge and enterprise is called:
quiz.why: Knowledge and enterprise, needed to put land, labour and capital to use and produce an output, is called human capital.

quiz.q: How many families live in Palampur (approx.)?
quiz.why: Palampur has about 450 families, belonging to various castes, and about one-third of them are landless.

lessons.title: Farming in Palampur: land and multiple cropping

scenes.text: In the rainy season (kharif), farmers grow jowar and bajra. Between October and December, potato.
In winter (rabi), wheat. A part of the land also grows sugarcane, harvested once a year. Same land, more output.

steps.title: Land is fixed
steps.body:
75% of the people of Palampur depend on farming. **Land area under cultivation is practically fixed**; since 1960 no new land has been brought under cultivation in Palampur. Standard unit of measuring land is the **hectare** (a square with sides of 100 m = 10,000 sq m).

To grow more on the same land, two ways:
1. **Multiple cropping** — growing more than one crop on a piece of land during the year; the most common way of increasing production.
2. **Modern farming methods** for higher yield.

steps.title: Multiple cropping in Palampur
steps.body:
- **Kharif** (rainy season): **jowar and bajra** (cattle feed).
- **October–December**: **potato**.
- **Rabi** (winter): **wheat** — some for the family, surplus sold at Raiganj market.
- Part of land under **sugarcane** — harvested once a year; sold as raw sugarcane or jaggery (gur) to traders in Shahpur.
It is possible because of a **well-developed irrigation** system: electricity reached early and transformed irrigation — **electric tubewells** replaced Persian wheels. Note: in India, less than 40% of cultivated area is irrigated even today; elsewhere farming depends on rainfall.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Convert 2.5 hectares to square metres.** 2.5 × 10,000 = **25,000 sq m**.

**Ex 2. Yield comparison.** Traditional wheat yield 1,300 kg/ha; HYV yield 3,200 kg/ha. Extra on 2 ha = (3,200 − 1,300) × 2 = **3,800 kg**.

**Ex 3. Why can Palampur farmers grow three crops but many villages only one?** Assured irrigation from electric tubewells vs dependence on rainfall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 1 hectare = 10,000 sq m (100 m × 100 m), not 1,000.
- Multiple cropping ≠ mixed cropping. Multiple = several crops **one after another** in a year.
- Jowar and bajra are **kharif**; wheat is **rabi**.

activity.prompt: A farmer has 3 hectares. How many square metres is that?

quiz.q: 1 hectare equals:
quiz.why: One hectare is a square of 100 m × 100 m, which is 10,000 sq m.

quiz.q: The most common way of increasing production on fixed land:
quiz.why: Multiple cropping, growing more than one crop on a piece of land in a year, is the most common way to increase production on fixed land.

quiz.q: Which crop is grown in rabi season in Palampur?
quiz.why: Wheat is the rabi (winter) crop in Palampur. Jowar and bajra are kharif crops, and rice is also a kharif crop.

quiz.q: Palampur's irrigation is mainly by:
quiz.why: Palampur's farmers mainly irrigate with electric tubewells, which replaced the Persian wheel. They made multiple cropping possible.

quiz.q: Jowar and bajra are used mainly as:
quiz.why: In Palampur, jowar and bajra are grown in the rainy season and are used mainly as cattle feed, not as cash or export crops.

lessons.title: Green Revolution, land distribution, labour and capital

scenes.text: Savita, a small farmer with 1 hectare, needs money for seeds and fertilisers. Banks are far and ask for papers.
She borrows from Tejpal Singh, a large landowner, at 24% interest for four months, and must also work on his field at low wages.

steps.title: The Green Revolution
steps.body:
In the late 1960s the **Green Revolution** introduced farmers to cultivation of wheat and rice using **high yielding varieties (HYV)** of seeds. HYV seeds promised much greater grain per plant but needed plenty of water, **chemical fertilisers and pesticides**. Farmers of **Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh** were the first to try it. Some also used tractors and threshers. In Palampur, yield of wheat grown from traditional varieties was about **1,300 kg/ha**; with HYV seeds it went up to **3,200 kg/ha**.

**Sustainability concerns**: overuse of chemical fertilisers reduces soil fertility and kills micro-organisms; excess tubewell use has lowered the **water table** in many areas.

steps.title: Land, labour and capital in Palampur
steps.body:
- **Land distribution is unequal**: about one-third of the 450 families are landless (mostly dalits); 240 families cultivate small plots of less than 2 ha; about 60 families of medium and large farmers cultivate more than 2 ha, a few over 10 ha.
- **Labour**: small farmers and their families cultivate their own fields; medium and large farmers hire **farm labourers** — from landless or small-plot families, paid in cash or kind (crops) or meals, sometimes employed for a whole year. Wages are often below the government-set minimum wage because of heavy competition for work. (e.g. **Dala and Ramkali**, landless labourers.)
- **Capital**: small farmers borrow from large farmers, village moneylenders or traders at very high interest rates; medium and large farmers use their own savings.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Interest on Savita's loan.** Loan ₹3,000 at 24% per year for 4 months: Interest = 3,000 × 24/100 × 4/12 = **₹240**. (Plus she must work on Tejpal's land at low wages — a hidden cost.)

**Ex 2. Why are farm wages low in Palampur? (2 marks)** Many landless labourers compete for limited work; they accept low wages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Green Revolution began in the **late 1960s**, mainly for **wheat and rice**.
- HYV seeds need **more** water and fertiliser, not less.
- Large farmers use savings from surplus; small farmers **borrow**.

activity.prompt: A farmer borrows ₹5,000 at 24% per year for 6 months. What is the simple interest?

quiz.q: The Green Revolution introduced:
options: HYV seeds for wheat and rice
quiz.why: The Green Revolution introduced HYV (high yielding variety) seeds for wheat and rice, along with fertilisers and irrigation, to raise yields.

quiz.q: Which states first adopted the Green Revolution?
quiz.why: Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh were the first to adopt the Green Revolution, as they had good irrigation. Kerala and Assam were not the first.

quiz.q: HYV wheat yield in Palampur:
quiz.why: HYV wheat in Palampur gave a yield of about 3,200 kg per hectare, much more than the 1,300 kg of the old seeds.

quiz.q: A sustainability problem of the Green Revolution:
options: Falling water table and loss of soil fertility
quiz.why: Overuse of groundwater and chemical fertilisers led to a falling water table and loss of soil fertility. This is a sustainability problem of the Green Revolution.

quiz.q: Why do farm labourers accept wages below minimum?
quiz.why: Many labourers compete for limited farm work, so they accept wages below the minimum. The government does not require or pay this.

lessons.title: Surplus and non-farm activities

scenes.text: Kareem notices many Palampur students go to college in town. He opens a computer class with two computers and hires trained teachers.
Meanwhile Kishora, a farm labourer, buys a buffalo with a bank loan and a cart to transport goods. He now earns more.

steps.title: Selling the surplus
steps.body: Farmers keep some wheat for the family and sell the **surplus** at the market at Raiganj. Small farmers have little surplus. Large farmers sell more; they save a part of earnings to buy capital (machines) or lend to small farmers, or use it as working capital for non-farm activities. Thus capital for future production is arranged from farm earnings.

steps.title: Non-farm activities
steps.body:
Only about **25%** of Palampur's working people are engaged in non-farm activities.
- **Dairy**: people feed buffaloes on grass, jowar and bajra; milk sold in Raiganj; two traders from Shahpur have set up collection-cum-chilling centres.
- **Small-scale manufacturing**: simple methods at home or in fields with family labour (e.g. **Mishrilal** bought an electric sugarcane crushing machine and makes jaggery).
- **Shopkeepers**: buy goods from wholesale markets in cities and sell in the village (rice, wheat, sugar, tea, oil, biscuits, soap); a few open small shops near the bus stand.
- **Transport**: rickshawallahs, tongawallahs, jeep, tractor, truck drivers, bullock and buffalo carts carry people and goods (e.g. **Kishora**).
- **Education**: e.g. **Kareem's computer classes**.
Non-farm activities need little land but need **capital**; loans can come from banks or own savings. More non-farm activities would help the village grow.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Kishora's life change? (3 marks)** A farm labourer earning low wages, he took a government-sponsored bank loan to buy a buffalo; he uses a buffalo cart to transport goods and sells milk — earning more than before.

**Q2. Why is non-farm activity important for villages? (2 marks)** Land is fixed and many are landless; non-farm work gives extra income without needing land.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Only **25%** of workers are in non-farm activities — farming is still dominant.
- Kareem's centre shows **human capital** being used in services.

activity.prompt: Match the person or activity
pairs: Buys from city wholesale, sells in village

quiz.q: Share of Palampur workers in non-farm activities:
quiz.why: Only about 25% of Palampur's workers are engaged in non-farm activities, while most still depend on farming.

quiz.q: Mishrilal is involved in:
quiz.why: Mishrilal makes jaggery with a machine and sells it to traders, which is small-scale manufacturing, a non-farm activity.

quiz.q: Kishora got a loan from a:
quiz.why: Kishora got a loan from a bank under a government scheme to buy a buffalo for dairy. This is different from a loan from a moneylender.

quiz.q: Where do Palampur farmers sell surplus wheat?
quiz.why: Palampur's farmers sell their surplus wheat at the market in Raiganj, a nearby small town, to traders.

quiz.q: What do non-farm activities need most?
quiz.why: Non-farm activities need capital more than land, since they need little land. Many people lack the capital to start them.

questions.q: The four factors of production are land, labour, physical capital and:
questions.why: The four requirements of production are land, labour, physical capital and human capital. Money is not a separate factor.

questions.q: Which is a rabi crop?
questions.why: Wheat is a rabi crop sown in winter. Cotton, bajra and jowar are kharif crops.

questions.q: HYV stands for:
questions.why: HYV stands for High Yielding Variety seeds, which give higher yields than traditional seeds.

questions.q: Fixed capital example:
questions.why: Tools and machines are fixed capital, used in production for many years. Fertiliser, wages and seeds are used up quickly, so they are working capital.

questions.q: Multiple cropping means:
options: Growing many crops mixed together once
Growing more than one crop on the same land in a year
questions.why: Multiple cropping means growing more than one crop on the same land in a year. Mixed cropping is different, as it grows many crops together at once.

questions.q: Small farmers in Palampur mostly get capital from:
questions.why: Small farmers mostly borrow capital from large farmers or moneylenders at high interest, since they lack savings. They rarely get foreign aid.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Palampur farmers can grow three crops a year. Reason (R): They have assured irrigation from electric tubewells.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Assured irrigation from electric tubewells lets farmers grow three crops a year. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A landless labourer gets ₹250/day though the minimum wage is ₹350. The best explanation:
options: Many labourers compete for limited farm work
Wages are paid by the government
questions.why: When many labourers compete for limited farm work, labour supply exceeds demand, so wages are pushed below the minimum. Scarce labour would raise wages.

questions.q: Which is a sustainability concern of modern farming?
options: Overuse of groundwater lowering the water table
questions.why: Overuse of groundwater lowers the water table, which threatens sustainability. Manure, crop rotation and organic farming are sustainable practices.

questions.q: What share of Palampur's families are landless (approx.)?
questions.why: About 150 of 450 families in Palampur are landless, which is one-third. They work as farm labourers.

questions.q: Yield rises from 1,300 to 3,200 kg/ha. Percentage increase (approx.)?
questions.why: Increase = 3,200 − 1,300 = 1,900 kg. 1,900 ÷ 1,300 × 100 ≈ 146%. Divide the increase by the original value.

questions.q: ₹10,000 borrowed at 24% per year for 4 months. Interest?
questions.why: Interest = principal × rate × time = 10,000 × 0.24 × 4/12 = ₹800. The rate is yearly, so 4 months is 4/12 of a year.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Land is the most important scarce factor in Palampur. Reason (R): No new land has been brought under cultivation since 1960.
questions.why: Both are true. Land is fixed since no new land has been added since 1960, so it is the scarce factor. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A large farmer earns surplus and buys a tractor, then rents it to others. This shows:
options: Farm earnings becoming fixed capital for further production
questions.why: The farmer uses surplus farm earnings to buy a tractor, which is fixed capital used in later production. It is not working capital, which is used up.

questions.q: Which policy would most help Palampur's landless families?
options: Easy, cheap credit and more non-farm jobs
questions.why: Cheap credit and more non-farm jobs would raise the incomes of landless families. Ending schools or banning tubewells would hurt them.

courses.title: Ch 2 · People as Resource
courses.summary: How population becomes an asset through investment in education and health, the three sectors of activity, market and non-market work, women's work, and unemployment.
outcomes: Learners can explain human capital formation
Learners can classify activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors
Learners can explain the role of education and health
Learners can describe types of unemployment and their effects

lessons.title: Population as an asset; Sakal and Vilas

scenes.text: Sakal's mother keeps him in school and he trains in computer programming. He gets a job in a private firm and designs software.
Vilas, sickly and unable to go to school, sells fish like his mother and earns little. Same village, different lives.

steps.title: People as resource
steps.body:
'People as resource' refers to a country's working people in terms of their existing productive skills and abilities. Population becomes **human capital** when there is investment in it through **education, training and medical care** — this is **human capital formation**. Like land and physical capital, human capital adds to productivity; a skilled, healthy population can make better use of other resources.

Japan, with few natural resources, became rich by investing in people — especially education and health. Educated parents invest more in their children's education and health — a **virtuous cycle**; the reverse is a **vicious cycle**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Sakal and Vilas differ? (3 marks)** Sakal got education and training (investment in human capital) → software job, higher income. Vilas lacked education and health care → low-income fish selling. Shows the returns to human capital.

**Q2. How is human capital different from physical capital? (2 marks)** Human capital is knowledge and skills embodied in people (education, health); physical capital is machines and tools. Human capital can use physical capital better.

steps.title: Benefits of investment
steps.body: Investment in human capital yields returns just like investment in physical capital: higher incomes because of higher productivity. Benefits go not only to the individual but also to society (taxes, better health, innovation). India's Green Revolution and IT revolution show the importance of knowledge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A large population is not automatically a liability — it becomes an **asset** with investment.
- Human capital formation = education + training + health, not just 'more people'.

statements.s: A large population can be an asset if people are educated and healthy.
Japan became rich mainly because of huge natural resources.
Educated parents tend to invest more in their children — a virtuous cycle.
statements.why: Benefits pass to the next generation.

statements.s: Human capital refers only to machines.

quiz.q: Human capital formation means:
options: Investment in education, training and health
quiz.why: Human capital formation means investing in education, training and health, which makes people more productive. Printing money or buying land does not.

quiz.q: Which country is an example of growth through human capital?
quiz.why: Japan has few natural resources, but invested heavily in people, particularly education and health, and became developed. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait rely on oil.

quiz.q: Sakal's success came from:
quiz.why: Sakal succeeded because of his education and training, which made him more productive. This shows the value of human capital.

quiz.q: Why did Vilas earn little?
options: Lack of education and poor health
quiz.why: Vilas earned little because he lacked education and had poor health. Nobody had invested in his human capital.

quiz.q: Investment in human capital benefits:
quiz.why: Investment in human capital benefits both the individual, through higher income, and society, through growth and better services.

lessons.title: Economic activities: sectors, market and non-market

scenes.text: Anu's mother cooks, cleans and cares for the family all day — unpaid. Her father drives a bus and earns a salary.
Anu wonders: does the economy count her mother's work? Usually not — that's a big debate.

steps.title: Three sectors
steps.body:
- **Primary sector**: agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry, fishing, poultry farming, mining and quarrying.
- **Secondary sector**: manufacturing (and construction, electricity, gas and water supply).
- **Tertiary sector**: services — trade, transport, communication, banking, education, health, tourism, insurance.
The activities in these sectors result in production of goods and services; they add value to the **national income**.

steps.title: Market and non-market activities
steps.body:
- **Market activities**: involve remuneration to anyone who performs them — production of goods or services for sale, including government services.
- **Non-market activities**: production for **self-consumption** — consumption and processing of primary products and own-account production of fixed assets.

**Women's work**: due to historical and cultural reasons, there is a division of labour; women generally look after domestic chores and men work in fields. Household work is **not paid** and not recognised in national income. Women with high education and skills are paid at par with men; most women working in the unorganised sector get low pay and lack job security, legal protection, maternity leave, childcare and other benefits.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Classify: a fisherman, a car factory worker, a teacher. (3 marks)** Primary; secondary; tertiary.

**Q2. Why is women's household work not counted in national income? (2 marks)** It is not paid for (non-market) and is not sold in a market, so it is not measured, though it has real economic value.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mining is **primary**, not secondary.
- Government services (e.g. teaching in a government school) are **market** activities because they are paid.
- Unpaid ≠ unimportant: household work has great value.

activity.prompt: Sort the activities into sectors

quiz.q: Which sector includes mining?
quiz.why: Mining is a primary sector activity because it takes natural resources from the earth. Manufacturing is secondary and services are tertiary.

quiz.q: Banking belongs to:
quiz.why: Banking is part of the tertiary sector, which provides services. Primary sector produces from nature and secondary manufactures.

quiz.q: Production for self-consumption is a:
quiz.why: Production for self-consumption is a non-market activity because it is not sold in the market. Market activities involve pay or profit.

quiz.q: Household work by women is:
options: Unpaid and not counted in national income
quiz.why: Household work by women is unpaid and so it is not counted in national income, although it is valuable.

quiz.q: Manufacturing is part of the:
quiz.why: Manufacturing changes raw materials into goods, so it belongs to the secondary sector. Primary is raw material production and tertiary is services.

lessons.title: Quality of population: education and health

scenes.text: In a government school, Priya eats a hot mid-day meal. Her attendance has improved since the meal began.
Her teacher says: well-fed children learn better — education and health go together.

steps.title: Education
steps.body:
Education opens new horizons, provides new aspirations and develops values; it contributes to the growth of society, national income, cultural richness and efficiency of governance.
- Literacy rate in India rose from **18% in 1951** to about **74% in 2011**. Literacy is higher among males and in urban areas; it varies across states (Kerala highest, Bihar lowest in 2011).
- **Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan** (begun 2000–01): a step towards providing elementary education to all children aged **6–14** by a time-bound target, with state governments, local governments and the community. Now part of **Samagra Shiksha**.
- **Mid-day meal** scheme (now PM POSHAN): to encourage attendance and retention of children and improve their nutrition.
- Bridge courses, back-to-school camps; vocational streams in secondary education; growing higher education institutions.

steps.title: Health
steps.body:
The health of a person helps realise potential and ability to fight illness. An unhealthy person is a liability for an organisation. National policy aims to improve accessibility of health care, family welfare and nutritional services, with special focus on underprivileged segments.
- Over the years, India has built a vast health infrastructure: primary health centres, community health centres, dispensaries, hospitals.
- Life expectancy rose to about **68 years** (2011–15 data) and **infant mortality rate (IMR)** fell from **147 per 1,000 live births in 1951** to about **33** (around 2016–17), declining further since.
- Medical colleges, dental colleges and nursing institutions have expanded.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How does the mid-day meal scheme help? (2 marks)** Encourages enrolment and attendance; improves nutrition and concentration.

**Q2. Why is health important for human capital? (2 marks)** Healthy workers are more productive and lose fewer workdays; healthy children learn better.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- IMR = deaths of children **under one year** per 1,000 live births, not under five.
- SSA targets children **6–14**, not 3–18.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Average years a person is expected to live

quiz.q: Literacy rate in 1951 was about:
quiz.why: India's literacy rate in 1951 was only about 18%, and it rose to about 74% by 2011.

quiz.q: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan covers children aged:
quiz.why: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan aims at universal elementary education for children aged 6 to 14.

quiz.q: IMR measures deaths of children under:
quiz.why: The infant mortality rate (IMR) measures the deaths of children under one year of age per 1,000 live births.

quiz.q: Why was the mid-day meal introduced?
options: To encourage attendance and improve nutrition
quiz.why: The mid-day meal was introduced to encourage school attendance and improve children's nutrition. It does not close schools or raise fees.

quiz.q: IMR in India in 1951 was about:
quiz.why: India's IMR in 1951 was about 147 per 1,000 live births. It has fallen sharply since.

lessons.title: Unemployment

scenes.text: Five members of a family work on a small plot that needs only two workers.
If three move out to other jobs, the farm's output does not fall. They were 'disguisedly' unemployed.

steps.title: What is unemployment?
steps.body:
**Unemployment** exists when people who are willing to work at the going wages cannot find jobs. The workforce includes people aged **15–59**. Children, the very old and those unable to work are not counted as unemployed.

Types in **rural** areas:
- **Seasonal unemployment**: people cannot find jobs during some months of the year — e.g. farm workers after sowing and before harvest.
- **Disguised unemployment**: people appear to be employed, but more people are working on a job than needed; their contribution is nil. Common in agriculture, where the whole family works on a small plot.

In **urban** areas: **educated unemployment** — many youth with degrees cannot find jobs; there is unemployment among graduates and post-graduates, while there is a shortage of certain technical skills.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
- Wastage of manpower resource; people who are an asset turn into a liability.
- Feeling of hopelessness and despair among youth.
- Dependence of the unemployed on the working population increases.
- Negatively affects health and quality of life; overall economic growth suffers.
- Increase in unemployment is an indicator of a **depressed economy**.

In India, agriculture is the most labour-absorbing sector, but its dependence has decreased partly due to disguised unemployment; some surplus labour has moved to secondary and tertiary sectors; employment in the service sector has increased.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Disguised unemployment.** A farm needs 3 workers but 7 family members work. Disguised unemployed = 7 − 3 = **4**.

**Ex 2. Unemployment rate.** In a town, labour force = 50,000; employed = 46,000. Unemployed = 4,000. Rate = 4,000 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = **8%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A student or homemaker who is not seeking paid work is **not** counted as unemployed.
- Disguised unemployment: people **appear** employed; seasonal: no work for **some months**.

activity.prompt: Identify the type of unemployment

items.text: Farm labourer idle between sowing and harvest
Six family members on a field needing two
An engineering graduate cannot find a job
Workers at a sugar mill idle after the crushing season

quiz.q: Disguised unemployment is common in:
quiz.why: Disguised unemployment is common in agriculture, as more family members work on a farm than are needed. Banking and railways do not have it.

quiz.q: Seasonal unemployment occurs when:
options: People are idle in certain months
quiz.why: Seasonal unemployment occurs when people can find work only in some months of the year, like farm workers in the off-season.

quiz.q: Educated unemployment is common in:
quiz.why: Educated unemployment is common in urban areas, where educated youth cannot find jobs matching their qualifications.

quiz.q: The workforce age group in India is:
quiz.why: The working age group in India is 15–59 years, the people who can take part in production.

quiz.q: Labour force 20,000, employed 18,000. Unemployment rate?
quiz.why: Unemployed = 20,000 − 18,000 = 2,000. Rate = 2,000 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = 10%. The rate is based on the labour force.

questions.q: Which is a primary sector activity?
questions.why: Fishing takes a product from nature, so it is a primary sector activity. Manufacturing is secondary, and teaching and banking are services.

questions.q: Human capital is built through:
questions.why: Human capital is built through education, training and health, which raise productivity. Land and machines are physical resources.

questions.q: Disguised unemployment means:
questions.why: Disguised unemployment means more people work than are needed, so removing some wouldn't reduce output. Seasonal idleness is a different type.

questions.q: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan aims at education for children aged:
questions.why: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan aims to provide elementary education to children aged 6–14.

questions.q: Which is a non-market activity?
options: A farmer growing vegetables for own family
questions.why: A farmer growing vegetables only for his own family does not sell them, so it is a non-market activity. A driver, teacher and tailor earn pay in the market.

questions.q: Literacy rate of India in 2011:
questions.why: India's literacy rate in 2011 was about 74%.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Japan became developed despite few resources. Reason (R): It invested heavily in its people.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Japan has few resources but invested heavily in its people, building human capital, and so became developed. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A graduate in Lucknow applies for 50 jobs and gets none while companies say they can't find skilled technicians. This shows:
options: Educated unemployment with a skills mismatch
questions.why: A graduate with no job while firms cannot find technicians shows educated unemployment with a skills mismatch. It is not seasonal or disguised unemployment.

questions.q: Why is women's domestic work not counted in national income?
options: It is unpaid and not exchanged in the market
questions.why: Women's domestic work is unpaid and not exchanged in the market, so it is not counted in national income, although it has great value.

questions.q: Which is a consequence of unemployment?
options: Wastage of manpower and despair among youth
questions.why: Unemployment wastes manpower and causes despair among the youth. It does not raise savings or growth.

questions.q: A field needs 4 workers; 9 family members work there. How many are disguisedly unemployed?
questions.why: Workers needed = 4, but 9 work, so 9 − 4 = 5 are disguisedly unemployed. They add nothing to output.

questions.q: IMR fell from 147 to about 33 per 1,000. Percentage fall (approx.)?
Assertion (A): Removing disguisedly unemployed workers from a farm reduces output. Reason (R): Their marginal contribution to output is nil.
questions.why: The assertion is false because removing workers whose marginal contribution is nil leaves output unchanged. The reason is true, so only R is correct.

questions.q: Case: A village family's daughter completes nursing training and gets a hospital job; she pays for her brother's schooling. This is an example of:
questions.why: A daughter's training gives her a job, and her earnings pay for her brother's schooling, so the benefits pass on. This is a virtuous cycle of human capital.

questions.q: Which policy best reduces seasonal unemployment in villages?
options: Promote irrigation, multiple cropping and non-farm work like dairy and small industries
questions.why: Irrigation, multiple cropping and non-farm work like dairy and small industries give work throughout the year and reduce seasonal unemployment. Closing schools or banning irrigation would hurt.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Poverty as a Challenge
courses.summary: What poverty looks like, how the poverty line is estimated, which groups and states are most vulnerable, global trends, causes, and anti-poverty measures.
outcomes: Learners can describe social and economic dimensions of poverty
Learners can explain how the poverty line is estimated
Learners can identify vulnerable groups and inter-state disparities
Learners can explain causes and evaluate anti-poverty programmes

lessons.title: Faces of poverty and the poverty line

scenes.text: Ram Saran works in a flour mill near Ranchi. He earns about ₹1,500 a month on the days he finds work and cannot afford his children's schooling.
Lakha Singh, a landless labourer in a UP village, works for wages in kind and has no proper clothes or medical care. Both are poor.

steps.title: Dimensions of poverty
steps.body:
Poverty means hunger and lack of shelter; a situation where parents cannot send children to school or a sick person cannot afford treatment; lack of clean water and sanitation; lack of a regular job at a minimum decent level. It also means living with a sense of **helplessness**. About **one in five** persons in India was poor (2011–12).

Social scientists look at poverty through **indicators**: levels of income and consumption, and also **illiteracy, lack of general resistance due to malnutrition, lack of access to health care, lack of job opportunities, lack of access to safe drinking water and sanitation**.
- **Social exclusion**: poverty means poor people have to live only in a poor surrounding with other poor people, excluded from enjoying social equality (e.g. the caste system).
- **Vulnerability**: greater probability of being more adversely affected than others when bad times come — floods, earthquakes, job loss.

steps.title: The poverty line
steps.body:
A **poverty line** is an imaginary line that helps define poverty — a minimum level of income or consumption needed to fulfil basic needs (food, clothing, footwear, fuel, light, education, medical care).
- In India, the calorie requirement used was **2,400 calories per person per day in rural areas** and **2,100 in urban areas** (rural people do more physical work).
- For **2011–12**, the poverty line was fixed at **₹816 per person per month for rural areas** and **₹1,000 for urban areas** (Tendulkar method).
- Thus a family of five in rural areas living on less than about ₹4,080 per month would be below the poverty line.
- Poverty estimates are made periodically (usually every five years) using sample surveys by the **National Sample Survey Office (NSSO)**.
- For international comparisons, the **World Bank** uses a uniform international line — **$1.90 per person per day** (2011 PPP) in the textbook; the World Bank has since revised the figure upward.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Is a rural family of 4 earning ₹3,000 a month poor (2011–12 line)?**
Line for 4 = 4 × 816 = ₹3,264. ₹3,000 < ₹3,264 → **below the poverty line**.

**Ex 2. Urban family of 5 earning ₹5,500 a month?**
Line = 5 × 1,000 = ₹5,000. ₹5,500 > ₹5,000 → **above the line** (but still vulnerable).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rural calorie norm is **higher** (2,400) than urban (2,100) — because of heavier physical work.
- Poverty line is **per person per month**; multiply by family size.
- Being just above the line does not mean being well-off.

activity.prompt: Using ₹816 per person per month (rural, 2011–12), what is the poverty line for a rural family of 6?

quiz.q: Calorie norm for rural India:
quiz.why: The calorie norm used for the poverty line is 2,400 calories per person per day in rural areas. Urban areas use 2,100.

quiz.q: Rural poverty line 2011–12:
quiz.why: The poverty line in rural India for 2011–12 was ₹816 per person per month, as per the textbook.

quiz.q: Poverty surveys are conducted by:
quiz.why: Poverty estimates come from surveys by the NSSO (National Sample Survey Organisation). The RBI and Election Commission do not do this.

quiz.q: Vulnerability means:
options: Greater probability of being badly hit in bad times
quiz.why: Vulnerability means a greater probability of being badly hit in bad times, like floods or job loss, for certain groups.

quiz.q: Social exclusion means:
options: Being left out of social equality and opportunities
quiz.why: Social exclusion means being left out of equality and opportunities that others enjoy, for example because of caste. It can cause poverty.

lessons.title: Poverty estimates, vulnerable groups and inter-state disparities

scenes.text: Students look at data: poverty in India fell from about 45% in 1993–94 to about 22% in 2011–12.
But some states and groups remain far poorer. Their teacher asks: 'Why does progress reach some people slower?'

steps.title: Poverty estimates
steps.body: The poverty ratio in India declined from about **45% in 1993–94** to **37.2% in 2004–05**, and to about **22% in 2011–12** (Tendulkar method). The number of poor people also declined — from about **407 million (2004–05)** to about **270 million (2011–12)**. If the trend continues, India could eradicate extreme poverty in coming years.

steps.title: Vulnerable groups
steps.body:
Social groups most vulnerable: **Scheduled Castes** and **Scheduled Tribes** households.
Economic groups most vulnerable: **rural agricultural labour** households and **urban casual labour** households.
Poverty within families: inequality of incomes; women, elderly people and female infants are often systematically denied equal access to resources.

steps.title: Inter-state disparities
steps.body: The proportion of poor is not the same in every state. In 2011–12, the national average was about 22%. States such as **Odisha, Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh** had poverty above the national average; **Bihar and Odisha** remain among the poorest; Chhattisgarh had high rates. States with significant decline: **Kerala, Jammu & Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and West Bengal**; **Punjab and Haryana** succeeded through high agricultural growth; **Kerala** focused on human resource development; **West Bengal** on land reform; **Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu** on public distribution of foodgrains.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Percentage-point fall 1993–94 to 2011–12.** 45 − 22 = **23 percentage points**.

**Ex 2. Number of poor removed 2004–05 to 2011–12.** 407 − 270 = **137 million**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A fall in poverty **ratio** and a fall in the **number** of poor are different measures; both fell here.
- Kerala reduced poverty mainly through **human resource development**, not industrialisation.

activity.prompt: Match the state to its poverty-reduction route

quiz.q: Poverty ratio in India in 2011–12 was about:
quiz.why: The poverty ratio in India in 2011–12 was about 22%, down from about 45% in 1993–94.

quiz.q: Which social groups are most vulnerable to poverty?
quiz.why: SC and ST households are the most vulnerable social groups to poverty. Traders and large farmers are mostly better off.

quiz.q: Which state reduced poverty mainly through land reform?
quiz.why: West Bengal reduced poverty mainly through land reform measures. Punjab did so through agricultural growth, and Kerala through human resource development.

quiz.q: Within families, who suffer more from poverty?
quiz.why: Within families, women, the elderly and female infants often suffer most because of unequal access to resources.

quiz.q: Number of poor fell between 2004–05 and 2011–12 by about:
quiz.why: The number of poor fell from about 407 million in 2004–05 to about 270 million in 2011–12, which is 137 million fewer.

lessons.title: Global poverty and causes of poverty

scenes.text: In the 19th century, Indian handloom weavers lost work as cheap British mill cloth flooded markets.
Their great-grandchildren still face low incomes — history, policy and inequality shape poverty.

steps.title: Global poverty scenario
steps.body: The proportion of people in developing countries living in extreme poverty (World Bank definition) fell from about **36% in 1990** to about **10% in 2015**. Poverty declined substantially in **China** and **South-East Asian** countries as a result of rapid economic growth and massive investment in human resource development. In **South Asia** (India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan) the decline has also been rapid. In **Sub-Saharan Africa**, poverty fell from about 54% in 1990 to about 41% in 2015 — still very high. The UN's **Sustainable Development Goals** aim to end poverty of all types by **2030**.

steps.title: Causes of poverty in India
steps.body:
1. **Low level of economic development under British colonial rule**: policies ruined traditional handicrafts and discouraged industries like textiles.
2. **Low growth rate** until the 1980s, along with **high population growth** — per capita income grew slowly.
3. Failure of the Green Revolution and industrialisation to create enough jobs; **unemployment** high.
4. **Unequal distribution of land** and resources; land reforms poorly implemented.
5. **Socio-cultural factors**: the poor spend heavily on social obligations and religious ceremonies; poor farmers borrow from moneylenders at high rates and fall into **indebtedness**.
6. Huge **income inequalities**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did colonial rule cause poverty? (2 marks)** British policies ruined traditional handicrafts and discouraged industry, leaving many without livelihood.

**Q2. Why did China reduce poverty fast? (2 marks)** Rapid economic growth and massive investment in human resources (education and health).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Population growth alone is not the only cause — inequality, low growth and colonial history also matter.
- SDG target year for ending poverty is **2030**.

activity.prompt: Tick the causes of poverty in India discussed in the chapter
items: Colonial policies that ruined handicrafts
Low growth rate with high population growth
Unequal distribution of land
Indebtedness from high-interest loans
Social customs that push families into spending they can't afford

quiz.q: Global extreme poverty in developing countries fell from about 36% (1990) to:
quiz.why: Extreme poverty in developing countries fell from about 36% in 1990 to about 10% in 2015.

quiz.q: Which region still has very high poverty?
quiz.why: Sub-Saharan Africa still has very high poverty. East Asia has reduced it greatly, and Europe and North America have low poverty.

quiz.q: SDGs aim to end poverty by:
quiz.why: The Sustainable Development Goals aim to end poverty in all forms by 2030.

quiz.q: Which colonial policy increased poverty?
quiz.why: Colonial policies ruined traditional handicrafts, such as textiles, and left many artisans without work, increasing poverty.

quiz.q: Indebtedness among the poor is caused by:
options: Borrowing from moneylenders at high interest
quiz.why: The poor often borrow from moneylenders at high interest, which causes indebtedness. Low-interest bank loans, insurance and savings help them.

lessons.title: Anti-poverty measures and the challenges ahead

scenes.text: Under MGNREGA, Shanti digs a village pond for wages during the dry months when there is no farm work.
The pond helps irrigation and her family has income. One-third of such jobs are meant for women.

steps.title: Two-pronged strategy
steps.body: India's anti-poverty strategy is based on: (1) **promotion of economic growth** — growth widens opportunities and provides resources for human development; and (2) **targeted anti-poverty programmes**. Since the 1980s India's economic growth has been among the fastest; it has helped reduce poverty. But growth alone has not reached the poorest, so targeted schemes are needed.

steps.title: Major schemes
steps.body:
- **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005**: provides **100 days of assured wage employment** every year to every rural household; **one-third** of jobs reserved for women; if work is not provided within 15 days, an **unemployment allowance** is given. Central and state governments set up funds.
- **Prime Minister Rozgar Yojana (PMRY), 1993**: self-employment for educated unemployed youth in rural areas and small towns.
- **Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP), 1995**: self-employment in rural areas and small towns.
- **Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), 1999**: bring assisted poor families above the poverty line by organising them into **self-help groups** through bank credit and government subsidy.
- **Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY), 2000**: additional central assistance to states for basic services like primary health, primary education, rural shelter, drinking water and rural electrification.
- **Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY)**: food for the poorest (see Food Security).
- Later programmes: **National Rural Livelihoods Mission (Aajeevika, 2011)**, **Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014)**.

steps.title: Results and challenges
steps.body: Mixed results: a major reason for less effectiveness is lack of proper implementation and right targeting; overlapping schemes. The challenges ahead: providing health care, education and job security for all, achieving gender equality and dignity for the poor. Poverty is now seen more broadly — the idea is moving towards **human poverty** and **well-being**: being well-fed, healthy, literate and free from exclusion.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. State three features of MGNREGA. (3 marks)** 100 days' guaranteed wage employment per rural household per year; one-third jobs for women; unemployment allowance if work isn't given within 15 days.

**Q2. Why have anti-poverty programmes had mixed results? (2 marks)** Poor implementation, wrong targeting, overlapping schemes and leakages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- MGNREGA year is **2005**, guaranteeing **100** days (not 150).
- PMRY (1993) vs REGP (1995) vs SGSY (1999) vs PMGY (2000) — learn with years.

activity.prompt: Order these anti-poverty programmes

quiz.q: MGNREGA guarantees how many days of work per household per year?
quiz.why: The MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage employment per household per year in rural areas.

quiz.q: MGNREGA was enacted in:
quiz.why: MGNREGA, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, was passed in 2005.

quiz.q: SGSY organises the poor into:
quiz.why: The Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) organises the rural poor into self-help groups and gives them loans for self-employment.

quiz.q: Share of MGNREGA jobs reserved for women:
quiz.why: One-third of the jobs under MGNREGA are reserved for women.

quiz.q: India's anti-poverty strategy is based on growth and:
quiz.why: India's anti-poverty strategy has two parts: promoting economic growth and targeted anti-poverty programmes.

questions.q: Urban calorie norm:
questions.why: The calorie norm for the urban poverty line is 2,100 per person per day. For rural areas it is 2,400, because rural people do more physical work.

questions.q: MGNREGA provides:
questions.why: MGNREGA gives 100 days of wage employment a year to rural households. It does not give free houses, food or pensions.

questions.q: The World Bank international poverty line in the textbook:
questions.why: The World Bank's international poverty line in the textbook is $1.90 a day, in 2011 PPP terms. Later revisions have raised it.

questions.q: Which group is most vulnerable to poverty?
questions.why: Rural agricultural labourers are the most vulnerable to poverty, as they have no land and work only seasonally. Officers, professionals and large farmers are better off.

questions.q: PMRY was started in:
questions.why: The Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) was started in 1993 to create self-employment for educated unemployed youth.

questions.q: Which state reduced poverty mainly through high agricultural growth?
questions.why: Punjab and Haryana reduced poverty mainly through high agricultural growth. Kerala did so through human resource development.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The rural calorie norm is higher than urban. Reason (R): Rural people do more physical work.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Rural people do more physical work, so they need more energy, which is why the rural calorie norm is higher. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A family is just above the poverty line, but a flood destroys their crop and they fall below it. This illustrates:
questions.why: A family just above the poverty line that falls below it after a flood shows vulnerability: a greater chance of being hurt in bad times.

questions.q: Which is NOT a cause of poverty discussed in the chapter?
questions.why: High literacy helps reduce poverty, so it is not a cause. Unequal land distribution, high population growth and colonial policies are causes.

questions.q: Which programme provides extra central help for primary health, education, shelter and drinking water?
questions.why: The Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY), started in 2000, gives additional central assistance to states for primary health, education, housing and drinking water.

questions.q: Using ₹1,000 per person per month (urban), is an urban family of 4 earning ₹4,200 below the line?
questions.why: The family line = 4 × ₹1,000 = ₹4,000 per month. Its income of ₹4,200 is higher than that, so it is not below the line.

questions.q: If India's population is 1,250 million and poverty ratio 22%, the number of poor is about:
questions.why: Number of poor = 22% of 1,250 million = 0.22 × 1,250 = 275 million.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Economic growth alone is enough to remove poverty. Reason (R): Since the 1980s growth reduced poverty.
questions.why: The assertion is false because growth alone is not enough; targeted schemes are needed too. The reason is true, since growth has reduced poverty since the 1980s, so only R is correct.

questions.q: Case: A village gets work under MGNREGA but wages are paid late and fake names appear on rolls. Which challenge is this?
questions.why: Late wages and fake names on the rolls show poor implementation and leakages, a challenge to anti-poverty programmes. It is not about too much growth or land.

questions.q: Which broader idea of poverty is the chapter moving towards?
options: Human poverty and well-being (health, education, dignity, inclusion)
questions.why: The chapter moves toward a broader idea of human poverty, including health, education, dignity and inclusion, not just income or calories.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Food Security in India
courses.summary: What food security means, who is food-insecure, how India became self-sufficient in foodgrains, and how buffer stock, PDS, the NFSA and cooperatives provide food security.
outcomes: Learners can define food security and its three dimensions
Learners can identify food-insecure groups and types of hunger
Learners can explain self-sufficiency, buffer stock and MSP
Learners can describe the PDS, NFSA, AAY and the role of cooperatives

lessons.title: What is food security and why is it needed?

scenes.text: A drought hits a district. Crops fail; food prices shoot up. Daily wage earners cannot afford enough food.
Government fair price shops selling grain at low prices keep families from starving.

steps.title: Dimensions of food security
steps.body:
**Food security** means availability, accessibility and affordability of food to **all people at all times**.
- **Availability**: food production within the country, food imports and the previous years' stock stored in government granaries.
- **Accessibility**: food is within reach of every person.
- **Affordability**: an individual has enough money to buy sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet dietary needs.
A nation is food-secure only if enough food is available for all, all have the capacity to buy food of acceptable quality, and there is no barrier to access.

steps.title: Why food security is needed
steps.body:
The poorest may be food-insecure most of the time, while those above the line may become food-insecure during a **calamity** — drought, flood, earthquake, tsunami. A calamity reduces food production, creates shortage, raises prices; some people cannot buy food. If a calamity is widespread or lasts long it may cause **famine** — widespread deaths by starvation and epidemics caused by contaminated water or decaying food and loss of resistance.

The most devastating famine in India was the **Bengal Famine of 1943**, which killed about **30 lakh** people in the province of Bengal.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What are the dimensions of food security? (3 marks)** Availability (production, imports, stock), accessibility (within reach of all), affordability (enough money to buy sufficient nutritious food).

**Q2. How does a calamity affect food security? (3 marks)** Production falls → shortage → prices rise → poor cannot afford food → if prolonged, famine.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Food security is not just production — **access** and **affordability** matter equally.
- The Bengal Famine was **1943**, not 1947.

activity.prompt: Which dimension of food security?

items.text: A ration shop is within walking distance of a remote village
A labourer earns enough to buy dal and rice
Rice is imported after a bad harvest

quiz.q: Food security includes availability, accessibility and:
quiz.why: Food security has three dimensions: availability, accessibility and affordability. Affordability means people can afford enough nutritious food.

quiz.q: The Bengal Famine occurred in:
quiz.why: The Bengal Famine occurred in 1943, during the Second World War.

quiz.q: About how many died in the Bengal Famine?
quiz.why: About 30 lakh people died in the Bengal Famine of 1943, mostly from starvation and epidemics.

quiz.q: A famine is characterised by:
options: Widespread deaths by starvation and epidemics
quiz.why: A famine is marked by widespread deaths by starvation and epidemics, due to food shortage. Low prices, exports and surplus food do not describe it.

quiz.q: Availability of food depends on production, imports and:
quiz.why: Food availability depends on production within the country, imports and stocks carried over from previous years in government granaries.

lessons.title: Who are food-insecure? Hunger and self-sufficiency

scenes.text: Ramu, an agricultural labourer, has work only during sowing and harvesting. In other months his family often eats one meal.
When he gets work under a government scheme, his family can eat twice a day.

steps.title: Food-insecure groups
steps.body:
- In **rural areas**: landless people with little or no land, traditional artisans, providers of traditional services, petty self-employed workers and destitutes including beggars.
- In **urban areas**: families whose working members are employed in ill-paid occupations and casual labour markets.
- **SCs, STs and some OBCs** (lower castes) with poor land base or low land productivity.
- People affected by natural disasters who migrate in search of work.
- **Pregnant and nursing mothers and children under 5** — a large proportion suffer from malnutrition.
- Food-insecure people are disproportionately large in some regions: economically backward states with high poverty, tribal and remote areas, regions prone to natural disasters. States like **Uttar Pradesh (eastern and south-eastern parts), Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra** account for the largest number of food-insecure people.

steps.title: Hunger
steps.body:
**Hunger** is an aspect indicating food insecurity — not just an expression of poverty; it brings about poverty.
- **Chronic hunger**: a consequence of diets persistently inadequate in quantity and/or quality; poor people suffer it because of very low income.
- **Seasonal hunger**: related to cycles of food growing and harvesting; prevalent in rural areas because of the seasonal nature of agricultural activities, and in urban areas because of casual labour (e.g. less work in the rainy season).
The percentage of seasonal and chronic hunger has declined in India.

steps.title: Self-sufficiency in foodgrains
steps.body: After Independence, Indian policy-makers aimed at self-sufficiency. India adopted a new strategy — the **Green Revolution** — especially in wheat and rice. **Indira Gandhi** officially recorded the impressive strides by releasing a special stamp titled **'Wheat Revolution'** in **July 1968**. The success of wheat was later replicated in rice. Punjab and Haryana recorded the highest growth (wheat output rose from about 7.23 million tonnes in 1964–65 to an all-time high of over 30 million tonnes in later years). Since the advent of the Green Revolution, the country has avoided famine even during adverse weather conditions.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Distinguish chronic and seasonal hunger. (2 marks)** Chronic: persistently inadequate diet due to very low income. Seasonal: related to farming cycles or casual work availability.

**Q2. Why are children under 5 and pregnant women food-insecure? (2 marks)** They have high nutritional needs and often lack access to adequate food and health care.

statements.s: Seasonal hunger is linked to cycles of food growing and harvesting.
statements.why: Work and food vary by season.

statements.s: India has faced several famines since the Green Revolution.
statements.why: It has avoided famine since then.

statements.s: A 'Wheat Revolution' stamp was released in 1968.
Only urban people suffer chronic hunger.

quiz.q: Chronic hunger results from:
options: Persistently inadequate diet due to low income
quiz.why: Chronic hunger results from a persistently inadequate diet due to low income. Seasonal hunger happens only in some seasons.

quiz.q: The 'Wheat Revolution' stamp was released in:
quiz.why: The 'Wheat Revolution' stamp was released in July 1968, to mark the success of the Green Revolution in wheat.

quiz.q: Which crop first saw the Green Revolution's success?
quiz.why: The Green Revolution first succeeded in wheat, as production rose sharply in Punjab and Haryana. Rice followed.

quiz.q: Which group is especially food-insecure?
quiz.why: Children under 5 are especially food-insecure because they have high nutritional needs and are dependent on others. Bank managers and exporters are better off.

quiz.q: Seasonal hunger in urban areas is linked to:
options: Casual labour with less work in some seasons
quiz.why: Seasonal hunger in urban areas is linked to casual labour, as they get less work in some seasons, so their income falls.

lessons.title: Buffer stock, MSP and the Public Distribution System

story.title: From farm to fair price shop

scenes.text: A Punjab farmer sells wheat to the Food Corporation of India at the minimum support price announced before sowing.
Months later, that wheat reaches a ration shop in Odisha and is sold at a low issue price to poor families.

steps.title: Buffer stock and MSP
steps.body:
**Buffer stock** is the stock of foodgrains, namely wheat and rice, procured by the government through the **Food Corporation of India (FCI)**. The FCI purchases wheat and rice from farmers in states where there is surplus production.
- Farmers are paid a pre-announced price called the **Minimum Support Price (MSP)**, declared by the government every year **before the sowing season** to give incentives to raise production.
- Purchased grain is stored in granaries. Buffer stock is used to distribute foodgrains in deficit areas and among the poorer strata at a price lower than the market price, called the **issue price**. It also helps resolve shortages during adverse weather or calamity.

steps.title: Public Distribution System (PDS)
steps.body:
Food procured by the FCI is distributed among the poorer sections through government-regulated **ration shops** (also called **fair price shops**), which stock foodgrains, sugar and kerosene for cooking, sold at lower than market prices. Any family with a **ration card** can buy a stipulated amount each month.
- Ration cards: **Antyodaya cards** for the poorest of the poor, **BPL cards** for those below the poverty line, and **APL cards** for others.
- Rationing began in India in the **1940s** against the backdrop of the Bengal famine; revived in the 1960s during acute food shortage before the Green Revolution.
- In the 1970s three important programmes: **PDS**, **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** (1975, experimental basis) and **Food-for-Work (FFW)** (1977–78).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1. Saving through PDS.** Market price of rice ₹30/kg; issue price ₹3/kg. A family buys 35 kg. Saving = (30 − 3) × 35 = **₹945 per month**.

**Ex 2. Why is MSP announced before sowing? (2 marks)** To assure farmers of a price so they invest in growing more of the crop.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- MSP is the price paid **to farmers**; issue price is charged **to consumers** at ration shops.
- Buffer stock is mainly **wheat and rice**.
- ICDS began in **1975**; FFW in **1977–78**.

activity.prompt: Order the journey of grain through the food security system
items: Government announces MSP before sowing
Farmers grow and harvest wheat
FCI procures wheat at MSP
Wheat is stored as buffer stock
Grain sent to ration shops in deficit areas
Families with ration cards buy at the issue price

quiz.q: Buffer stock is maintained by:
quiz.why: The Food Corporation of India (FCI) buys foodgrains from farmers and keeps buffer stock. The RBI and NABARD do not do this.

quiz.q: MSP is announced:
quiz.why: The Minimum Support Price is announced before the sowing season so that farmers are assured of a price and encouraged to grow crops.

quiz.q: The price at which grain is sold at ration shops:
quiz.why: Grain is sold at ration shops at the issue price, which is lower than the market price. MSP is what farmers get from the government.

quiz.q: Ration card for the poorest of the poor:
quiz.why: Antyodaya cards are given to the poorest of the poor. BPL is for those below the poverty line and APL for those above.

quiz.q: ICDS was introduced in:
quiz.why: The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) was introduced in 1975 to improve the nutrition of young children and mothers.

lessons.title: TPDS, AAY, NFSA and the role of cooperatives

scenes.text: In Gujarat, Lakshmiben sells milk every morning to her village dairy cooperative, part of Amul.
The cooperative pays fairly and sells milk in cities. Cooperatives like this support food security too.

steps.title: Targeted schemes and the NFSA
steps.body:
- **Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), 1997**: adopted the principle of targeting the 'poor in all areas'; different prices for poor and non-poor.
- **Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY), December 2000**: 1 crore of the poorest among BPL families identified; **35 kg** of foodgrains per family per month at a highly subsidised rate of **₹2/kg for wheat and ₹3/kg for rice**. Later expanded.
- **Annapurna Scheme (APS), 2000**: for indigent senior citizens.
- **National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013**: provides food and nutritional security at affordable prices; categorises **75% of rural** and **50% of urban** population as eligible households; **5 kg** foodgrains per eligible person per month (AAY households continue to get 35 kg per family).
- Since 2023 foodgrains under NFSA are provided **free** under the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana framework (government decision).

steps.title: Current status and issues of PDS
steps.body:
PDS is the most important step by the government towards food security. It helped stabilise prices and made food available at affordable prices. Issues:
- FCI granaries were sometimes **overflowing** with grain, causing wastage and high storage costs, while some people still went hungry.
- **High MSP** encouraged farmers (especially in surplus states) to divert land from coarse grains to rice and wheat, and contributed to environmental degradation and falling water levels.
- **Malpractices**: ration shop dealers diverting grain to the open market, selling poor-quality grain, opening irregularly.
- The three-price system (Antyodaya, BPL, APL) left APL families with little incentive to buy from ration shops.

steps.title: Role of cooperatives
steps.body:
Cooperatives are playing an important role, especially in southern and western India.
- In **Tamil Nadu**, about **94%** of fair price shops are run by cooperatives.
- In **Delhi**, **Mother Dairy** provides milk and vegetables at controlled rates decided by the government.
- **Amul** (Gujarat) for milk and milk products — it brought about the **White Revolution**.
- In **Maharashtra**, the **Academy of Development Science (ADS)** facilitated a network of NGOs for setting up **grain banks** in different regions.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What does the NFSA 2013 provide? (3 marks)** Legal right to subsidised food for 75% rural and 50% urban population; 5 kg grain per person per month; AAY families 35 kg per family.

**Q2. Give two problems with PDS. (2 marks)** Overflowing granaries and wastage; malpractices by dealers like diverting grain to the open market.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- AAY: **35 kg per family**; NFSA: **5 kg per person**. Don't mix.
- Amul is in **Gujarat**; Mother Dairy in **Delhi**.

activity.prompt: Match the scheme or body
pairs: 35 kg per family for the poorest
Milk and vegetables at controlled rates in Delhi

quiz.q: AAY was launched in:
quiz.why: The Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) was launched in December 2000 to give subsidised grain to the poorest families.

quiz.q: Under AAY, rice was given at:
quiz.why: Under AAY, rice was given at ₹3 per kg and wheat at ₹2 per kg to the poorest families.

quiz.q: NFSA covers what share of the urban population?
quiz.why: The National Food Security Act covers 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.

quiz.q: In Tamil Nadu, about what share of fair price shops are run by cooperatives?
quiz.why: In Tamil Nadu, about 94% of fair price shops are run by cooperatives, so the PDS works well there.

quiz.q: The White Revolution is linked to:
quiz.why: The White Revolution, which raised milk production, is linked to Amul and the cooperative movement in Gujarat.

questions.q: FCI stands for:
questions.why: FCI stands for Food Corporation of India, which buys and stores foodgrains and keeps the buffer stock.

questions.q: Ration shops are also called:
questions.why: Ration shops are also called fair price shops, as they sell grain at fair, subsidised prices. Mandis are wholesale markets.

questions.q: The NFSA was passed in:
questions.why: The National Food Security Act (NFSA) was passed in 2013, giving a legal right to subsidised food grains.

questions.q: Which is a dimension of food security?
questions.why: Affordability is one dimension of food security, along with availability and accessibility. Automation, advertising and aviation are not.

questions.q: Minimum Support Price is paid to:
questions.why: The Minimum Support Price is paid to farmers by the government for their crops. It protects them from falling prices.

questions.q: Which programme began in 1977–78?
questions.why: The Food-for-Work programme began in 1977–78. ICDS began in 1975, and AAY in 2000.

questions.q: Assertion (A): India has avoided famine since the Green Revolution. Reason (R): Buffer stocks and increased production made food available even in bad years.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. India has avoided famine since the Green Revolution because buffer stocks and higher production kept food available even in bad years. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A ration dealer sells good wheat in the open market and gives poor families low-quality grain. Which issue is this?
questions.why: Selling good wheat in the open market and giving poor families low-quality grain is a malpractice in the PDS. It is a problem of implementation.

questions.q: Which statement about NFSA is correct?
options: Covers 75% rural and 50% urban; 5 kg per person
questions.why: NFSA covers 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population, with 5 kg of grain per person per month. The other statements are incorrect.

questions.q: Why did high MSP create problems?
options: Farmers shifted to rice/wheat from coarse grains; groundwater depleted; granaries overflowed
questions.why: High MSP made farmers shift to rice and wheat from coarse grains, depleted groundwater and led to overflowing granaries. These are its distortions.

questions.q: An AAY family buys 20 kg wheat at ₹2/kg and 15 kg rice at ₹3/kg. Total cost?
A household of 6 eligible persons under NFSA gets how much grain per month?
questions.why: Under NFSA each eligible person gets 5 kg of grain per month, so 6 persons get 6 × 5 = 30 kg.

questions.q: Assertion (A): APL families buy little from ration shops. Reason (R): Prices for APL were nearly the same as market prices, giving little incentive.
questions.why: Both are true. Prices for APL families were nearly the same as market prices, so there was little incentive to buy from ration shops. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: A drought-prone village in Maharashtra sets up a grain bank with NGO help. Which organisation facilitated such networks?
questions.why: The Academy of Development Science (ADS), an NGO in Maharashtra, helped villages set up grain banks. FCI, Amul and Mother Dairy are not in this role.

questions.q: Which combination best ensures food security for a poor rural family?
options: Availability through buffer stocks + access via nearby ration shops + affordability through subsidised prices and employment schemes
questions.why: Food security needs all three dimensions: availability via buffer stocks, access via nearby ration shops and affordability via subsidised prices and employment schemes. One alone is not enough.

lessons.title: History quick revision sheet

scenes.text: Aman has one evening to revise five History chapters. He panics.
His sister hands him a one-page sheet of dates and causes. 'Learn the skeleton first, then add flesh.'

steps.title: French Revolution

- 1774 Louis XVI · 5 May 1789 Estates General · 20 June Tennis Court Oath · 14 July Bastille · 4 Aug feudalism abolished · 1791 constitution · Apr 1792 war · 21 Sep 1792 republic · Jan 1793 king executed · 1793–94 Terror · Directory · 1804 Napoleon emperor · 1815 Waterloo · slavery 1794/1848 · women vote 1946.

steps.title: Russian Revolution

steps.title: Nazism

steps.title: Answer-writing technique
steps.body:
- **3 marks** = 3 distinct points, one line each, with one fact/date each.
- **5 marks** = intro line + 4–5 points + conclusion; use headings or numbering.
- Always include **a date, a name and a consequence**.

quiz.why: The Bastar rebellion took place in 1910. Waterloo was in 1815, Kristallnacht in 1938 and the Russian Revolution in 1917.

quiz.q: The Enabling Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The Enabling Act was passed in March 1933, giving Hitler the power to rule by decree.

quiz.q: Which river flows through a rift valley westward?
quiz.why: The Narmada flows west through a rift valley into the Arabian Sea. The Krishna, Kaveri and Godavari flow east.

quiz.q: The wettest place:
quiz.why: Mawsynram in Meghalaya has the highest average rainfall in the world, a little more than nearby Cherrapunji. Kochi and Mumbai are wet coastal cities but far less rainy.

quiz.q: Thorn forests grow where rainfall is:
quiz.why: Thorn forests and scrub grow in dry regions where annual rainfall is below 70 cm. Evergreen forests need over 200 cm and dry deciduous forests 70–100 cm.

quiz.q: Population density of India (2011):
quiz.why: India's population density in 2011 was 382 persons per sq km. Bihar's 1,102 is much higher, and Arunachal Pradesh's 17 is much lower.

quiz.q: IST is ahead of GMT by:
quiz.why: IST is based on 82°30′E. 82.5° × 4 minutes = 330 minutes, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

lessons.title: Political Science and Economics quick revision sheet

scenes.text: On the bus to school, Farhan flips flashcards: '14 days?' — 'Rajya Sabha delay on money bill!'
Short daily reviews beat one long night of cramming.

steps.title: Political Science
steps.body:
- Democracy: 4 features · Musharraf 1999, PRI till 2000, Saudi women 2015, Mugabe/ZANU-PF, China famine 1958–61.
- Mandela 28 yrs, Robben Island, 26 Apr 1994 · Constituent Assembly July/Dec 1946, 299 members, adopted 26 Nov 1949, in force 26 Jan 1950, Ambedkar · Preamble; 42nd Amendment 1976.
- 543 constituencies; SC 84, ST 47 · vote 18, contest 25 · EC; CEC appointed by President · MCC.
- Mandal: 1979/1980, OM 13 Aug 1990, 27%, Indira Sawhney 1992 · Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha (14 days) · President indirect; PM appointed · judicial review, PIL.
- Six Fundamental Rights; Art 17; 24-hour rule; NHRC 1993; RTI 2005; RTE 2009; property removed 1978.

steps.title: Economics
steps.body:
- Factors: land, labour, physical capital (fixed/working), human capital · 1 ha = 10,000 sq m · HYV 1,300 → 3,200 kg/ha · Green Revolution late 1960s.
- Sectors: primary/secondary/tertiary · market vs non-market · unemployment: seasonal, disguised, educated · literacy 18% → 74% · IMR 147 (1951).
- Poverty line 2011–12: ₹816 rural, ₹1,000 urban; 2,400/2,100 kcal · ~22% poor · MGNREGA 2005 (100 days), PMRY 1993, REGP 1995, SGSY 1999, PMGY 2000.
